Claude against ridge regression on FLIP2

One experiment, step by step: does a general-purpose language model that reads labeled protein variants in its prompt rank held-out variants better than ridge regression on protein language model features? Diego del Alamo asked for this test on 21 November 2026. The primer explains every piece in plain words, and each card below it is one question with its measurement and its result. Underlined terms open their definitions. Every number on the page is filled from the experiment's tables, scored on 22 November 2026. Cards M are Claude Mythos 5.2 through subagents, against controls and ESMC, and the last two set it against a protein language model that is tuned on the same rows, a comparison Diego del Alamo asked for on 23 November 2026: M13 is that comparison, and M14 asks whether the tuning was run at the right scale. Cards B are the baselines alone. Cards A are the Claude models on the public API, a separate experiment on other queries.

The question and the answer

The question, from Diego del Alamo's post: can someone with access to these models test in-context learning against ridge regression on protein language models, on the FLIP2 test cases, “because if that outperforms, then it's truly over”. A comment on the thread added that FLIP2 was public before these models were trained, so a good score could be memory. The experiment answers both.

No. In-context learning ties ridge regression on protein language models. It does not outperform it. Shown 256 labeled variants, Claude Mythos 5.2 reaches a mean Spearman of 0.38 (0.33 to 0.42) over the 16 FLIP2 splits. The best ridge on the same queries, on the ESMC-600M embedding, reaches 0.37 (0.32 to 0.41). The paired difference is +0.01 (−0.04 to +0.06). Its interval includes zero, and the rule fixed before launch calls that a tie (M1).

The tie holds where memory cannot help. On an FGFR2 screen published after the model's training data end, it scores 0.56 and the best ridge 0.57 (M3).

Tuning a protein language model on the same rows reaches the same level at best, and does not pass it. ProGen2-small, with every weight tuned on the 256 rows by a preference loss under the recipe set before the run, reaches 0.26, which is −0.12 (−0.16 to −0.07) from the language model and −0.10 (−0.16 to −0.05) from the best ridge (M13). That recipe let 51 held-out rows choose the setting and the stopping point, which cost about 0.07. With one setting run for 20 epochs and nothing chosen, ProGen2-small scores 0.32 (0.29 to 0.35) on queries 101 to 300 of each split, −0.03 (−0.06 to +0.01) from the best ridge there, and ProGen2-base, five times larger, scores 0.36 (0.31 to 0.40) on the first 100, −0.02 (−0.07 to +0.03) from the language model. Each of those intervals includes zero and none lies above it (M14).

The tie is an average of large wins and large losses. Split by split against that ridge: 3 of 16 ahead, 3 behind, 10 undecided (M2). The largest win is on Rhomax, which the model answers from what it already knows: it scores 0.66 there with no examples at all (M8, M9). Without Rhomax, a check added after the results were seen, the means are 0.36 for the model and 0.38 for the ridge.

The model learns from its prompt, and it also brings knowledge of the protein. Reverse the shown values and its ranking reverses on six of eight datasets (M6). Encipher the residues, so that the protein cannot be recognized, and its score falls from 0.50 to 0.28, near one-hot ridge at 0.21 (M5). Show it no examples and it scores 0.39, where the best zero-shot score of a protein language model is 0.32 (M7).

It has read about FLIP2, and it does not recite FLIP2's numbers. From 30 unlabeled rows it names the source study of all seven datasets (M10). Asked for the published values of the four datasets with continuous values, it wrote 0 of 400 exactly (M9).

It can write most of these proteins out, and that is not why it predicts them. With half the residues of a rhodopsin hidden it restores 76% of them, where ESMC-6B restores 54%. Its error on a rhodopsin does not depend on whether it could: the Spearman of the two is −0.15 (−0.41 to +0.13) (M12).

Use both. The average of the model's ranking and the ridge's scores 0.44, above either alone (M4). High effort did not reliably beat low effort (M11).

Every Claude Mythos 5.2 score rests on one prompt of 100 queries per split and one answer per prompt, asked through a coding agent's subagents.

The two language model parts are kept apart. Claude Mythos 5.2 was asked through subagents on the first 100 queries of each split, and the API models on all 300, so no figure and no card sets one beside the other. One observation says why they should not be: with no examples, at the level named low, the subagent route spent a median of 2,156 thinking tokens on a test prompt and the API route 0, and on the same seven splits and queries the scores are 0.39 and 0.22. That gap mixes the model with what surrounds its prompt (the two routes, effort).

Primer: what every piece is

Written for two readers at once: a protein scientist who has not called a language model through its API, and a machine learning reader who has not worked with mutational scans. Each entry builds on the one before. In every diagram and table, ochre marks something that is given and stays fixed during the experiment, and teal marks something a method computes.

A variant, its measured value, and a dataset

A variant is a protein sequence that differs from a reference sequence, the parent, at one or more positions. It is a string of one-letter amino acid codes. A measured value is one number that a laboratory assay gave for that variant, such as how active the enzyme is or how tightly it binds. A measured value is an experimental result. It is not a prediction, and nothing in this page turns a model's score into one.

A dataset is a table with one row per variant: the sequence and its measured value. The experiment uses the seven datasets of the FLIP2 benchmark and one dataset published after the language models were trained.

DatasetProteinWhat the assay measuredLengthHow its variants are written in a prompt
amylaseAlpha-amylase of Bacillus subtilisStain removal activity in a detergent assay425Substitutions against one parent
iredImine reductase of Streptosporangium roseumEnzyme activity in a microfluidic screen290Substitutions against one parent
nucbNuclease B of Bacillus licheniformisNuclease activity at pH 7, binned into levels 0 to 3142Substitutions against one parent
trpbBeta subunit of tryptophan synthaseGrowth-based fitness of combinatorial libraries389Substitutions against one parent
pdz3Third PDZ domain of PSD-95 with its CRIPT peptideBinding of the domain and peptide pair100 + 8Substitutions in either chain
hydroThree small domains: FYN SH3, chymotrypsin inhibitor 2, and CspAStability, with seven core residues randomized to F, I, L, M, or V57, 63, 65Whole sequences
rhomaxMicrobial rhodopsins, their variants and chimerasWavelength of peak light absorption, in nanometers227 to 365Whole sequences
fgfr2Kinase domain of human FGFR2, residues 461 to 780Resistance to the drug erdafitinib in a pooled screen, as a base-2 logarithm320Substitutions against one parent

A substitution is written as the parent's residue, the position, and the new residue: A12V means that position 12 holds A in the parent and V in the variant. A variant with several substitutions lists them with spaces, as in A12V G40D. Hydro and Rhomax have several parents of different lengths, so their variants are shown as whole sequences.

The first seven rows are FLIP2, read from flip.protein.properties on 2026-11-21. The last is MaveDB score set urn:mavedb:00001329-a-3, published on 2026-11-20, five months after the models' June 2026 training cutoff.

A split: which rows a method may learn from, and which it is tested on

A split is a rule that sorts a dataset's rows into a training part, a validation part, and a test part. It is a fixed list that comes with the benchmark, and it is not a model. A method may read the measured values of training rows. It is scored on test rows, whose measured values it never sees. Validation rows are for choosing settings before the test rows are touched.

FLIP2's splits are built to be hard in a specific way: the test rows differ from the training rows by design, the way a real engineering campaign moves away from what was already measured. The table says how, in words taken from what each split file holds.

SplitTraining rowsTest rowsHow the test rows differ from the training rows
amylase/by_mutation2,403702Every test variant carries at least one substitution that no training variant has.
amylase/close_to_far1,4261,924Test variants are mutated at positions that no training variant touches.
amylase/far_to_close1,5391,782The same, with the two groups of positions exchanged.
amylase/one_to_many2,574488Training variants carry 3.2 substitutions on average, and every test variant carries exactly one.
ired/two_to_many3,7464,178Training variants carry one or two substitutions, and test variants carry up to 15.
nucb/two_to_many2,08848,304Training variants carry one substitution and take only three activity levels, and test variants carry up to 23.
trpb/one_to_many304227,918Training variants carry at most one substitution, and test variants carry up to four.

Two files differ from the benchmark site's text: amylase/one_to_many trains on variants with several substitutions and tests on single substitutions, and nucb/two_to_many trains on single substitutions only. The experiment follows the files.

A task: the same labeled rows and the same questions for every method

A task is one fair contest on one split. It is a list of rows, not a model. It fixes k training rows whose measured values are shown, called the labeled rows, and q = 300 test rows whose values are withheld, called the queries. Every method receives exactly these rows and nothing else from the split, so a method cannot win by having seen more data.

  1. Draw the labeled rows. The training rows are put in a random order fixed by a seed, and the first k are taken. A smaller k is therefore a subset of a larger one. Most arms use k = 256.
  2. Draw the queries. 300 test rows are drawn once per split (184 for Rhomax, which has no more). Every arm and every method answers the same 300.
  3. Round the values. Shown values are rounded to a fixed number of decimals per split, and every baseline is fit on the rounded values, so no method sees more digits than another.
  4. Score. Each method returns one number per query, and the 300 numbers are compared with the 300 measured values by rank correlation.

Spearman rank correlation: the score

Spearman's ρ is one number between −1 and 1 computed from two lists of the same length. It is a score for a set of predictions, not a property of one prediction. It asks whether a method puts the queries in the same order as the laboratory did, and it ignores the scale of the predictions, which matters because a likelihood score and an activity value are not in the same units.

  1. Rank each list. Replace every measured value by its rank among the measured values, and every prediction by its rank among the predictions. Tied values share the mean of their ranks.
    r = rank(y)s = rank(ŷ)
  2. Correlate the ranks. Take the ordinary (Pearson) correlation of the two rank lists.
    ρ = corr(r, s)
    With no ties this equals 1 − 6 Σdi2 / (q(q2 − 1)), where di = ri − si.
QueryMeasured yRank rPredicted ŷRank sd
Q10.1021220
Q20.4043031
Q30.353414−1
Q40.8055550
Q50.051910

Made-up numbers. Σd2 = 2, so ρ = 1 − 12/120 = 0.90, although the predictions are on a different scale from the measurements. A value of 0 means the order is unrelated, and a negative value means it is reversed.

The experiment also reports three views of the top of the ranking. The top tenth of the queries by measured value are called hits, and a method is scored on how well its numbers separate hits from the rest: the area under the ROC curve (ROC AUC), the area under the precision-recall curve (PR AUC), and the balanced Matthews correlation coefficient (balanced MCC). These matter when the goal is to pick the best few variants, not to order all of them.

In-context learning: a language model that reads its examples in the prompt

A general-purpose language model is a neural network whose weights were fixed when its training ended. In-context learning is a way of using it, not a way of training it: the labeled rows are written into the text of the request, the prompt, and the model writes its predictions as text. No weight changes, nothing is stored between requests, and each request starts from the same model.

  1. Write the prompt. The prompt is one message with five parts, in this order: two sentences that say what the lines are, the parent sequence, the k labeled rows as variant <tab> value, 100 queries as identifier <tab> variant, and the reply format. It holds no example of reasoning and no hint about how to predict.
  2. Give it to the model. The 300 queries of a task go in three prompts of 100, which share the same first four parts. Each prompt is answered on its own, by a model that has seen none of the others. How a prompt reaches each model is the subject of the next entry.
  3. Read the reply. The model writes 100 lines of identifier <tab> number. A line that cannot be read as a number counts as unanswered, and an unanswered query is given the median of the shown values, so skipping hard queries cannot raise a score.
QuantityWhat it isKindSizeFor amylase/by_mutation at k = 256
Model weightsEverything the model learned in its own trainingfixednot publicnot public
Shared part of the promptInstruction, parent, and labeled rowsfixedgrows with k4,030 tokens
Queries and reply format100 identifiers and variantsfixed100 lines1,497 tokens
ThinkingText the model may write for itself before answering, not kept as an answercomputed0 or more tokensThrough the API: 0 at low effort, about 3,250 at high
Reply ŷ100 predicted valuescomputed100 linesabout 800 tokens

A token is the unit a language model reads and writes, a few characters long. A protein sequence costs about 0.93 tokens per residue. Effort is a setting of an API request that tells the model how much to think before it answers. At low effort the API models in this experiment wrote no thinking at all and answered in under ten seconds, which is the closest thing to a single pass of pattern completion. At high effort they wrote thousands of tokens of reasoning first.

Two routes to a model: a subagent, and the API

A route is the way a prompt reaches a model and its answer comes back. It is not part of the model, but it decides what else sits in front of the model beside the prompt. This experiment uses two. Claude Mythos 5.2, the model the results are about, is reached through subagents. Four other Claude models were reached earlier through the Messages API, the programming interface that returns one reply to one request.

A subagent is a new conversation that a coding agent starts with the same model. It begins with none of the main conversation: it knows only its own instruction. The steps for one prompt:

  1. Put the prompt in a file. Each prompt is written to prompt.txt in a folder named only by a number, so the path says nothing about the protein or the arm. The text is byte for byte what the API route sent.
  2. Start a fresh subagent with one instruction. The instruction is the same for every prompt, and says nothing about proteins or about what is being tested: “Read the file … in full. It holds a task and says how to reply. Write your reply, exactly in the form the task asks for and with nothing else, to … with the Write tool. Use no other tools: do not run code or commands, search, or open any other file. … When the file is written, reply with the single word done.”
  3. The subagent reads and answers. It reads the file, writes answer.txt beside it, and stops. One subagent answers one prompt and is never used again.
  4. Audit the transcript. The coding agent keeps a record of everything a subagent did. From it we read which model answered and every tool the subagent called. Reading its own prompt and writing its own answer are the protocol. Anything else, such as running code to fit a regression, is a breach: the answer is set aside and the prompt is asked once more by a new subagent.
  5. Score the answer file exactly as an API reply is scored.
What sits around the promptSubagent route (Claude Mythos 5.2)API route (the four other models)
Text before the promptThe coding agent's own system prompt and this workspace's instructions, which say the user studies protein machine learning and hold no measured valueNone
ToolsPresent, forbidden by the instruction, and checked in the transcriptNone
ThinkingSet by us as one of five effort levels, and read back from the transcriptSet by the effort of the request: low or high
A request the provider blocksWould leave no answer fileComes back marked as a refusal (see refusals)
Proof of which model answeredThe model named in the transcriptThe model named in the reply

What the subagent route costs, and what that did to the design. A subagent processes the coding agent's instructions on every step it takes, so even a prompt of a thousand tokens used 71,000 to 79,000 tokens here, and a long one up to 183,000. The account's usage limit stopped the subagents partway through the first evening. The plan was then cut, in writing and before any test answer of Claude Mythos 5.2 was scored, to what the question needs: every task is asked its first prompt only, which holds the first 100 of its queries, and the controls run on one split per dataset, called the probe splits on this page. Every comparison with Claude Mythos 5.2 scores the baselines on those same 100 queries. The API models answered every query of every arm, so their cards use all 300.

Because the two routes differ in what surrounds the prompt, a gap between Claude Mythos 5.2 and an API model cannot be assigned to the model alone.

Effort: how much a model thinks before it answers

Effort is a setting given with a request. It is not part of the model's weights. It tells the model how much text to write for itself, called thinking, before it writes the answer, and thinking is never scored. A subagent can be given one of five levels: low, medium, high, extra high, and maximum. The level each subagent ran at is written in its transcript and was checked for every prompt.

More thinking takes longer, and nobody knows in advance whether it helps on this task. So the level is chosen by a rule fixed before any test row was read, and a second level is then run on test rows, so a reader can see what the choice left out.

  1. Sweep on validation rows. Three prompts whose 100 queries come from the validation part of three splits are asked at each level. Each answer gets a ρ, and each level gets the mean of its three, vlevel. Low, medium, and high answered all three prompts. Extra high answered two before the usage limit stopped it, and maximum returned nothing in ten minutes a prompt, so neither has a mean.
  2. Choose the lowest level that is close to the best.
    selected = the lowest level with vlevel ≥ max(v) − 0.02
    The tolerance of 0.02 keeps the rule from chasing noise, because three prompts cannot tell two levels apart more finely than that.
  3. Run everything at the selected level. Every arm and every probe on test rows uses it, and the question the experiment set out to answer is read at it.
  4. Test the choice on test rows. The plain 256-row arm is also asked at high effort on the probe splits, and the two levels are compared on the same 100 queries of each (card M11).
CaseLowMediumHighExtra highMaximumSelectedWhy

Made-up validation means, one row per case. The rule can only pick a level that is too low by less than 0.02 on the validation prompts. It cannot see test rows, which is the point of it.

Refusals: a request that comes back with no answer

A refusal is a reply in which the provider's safety system stops the model before it answers. Through the API it is explicit: the reply carries a stop reason of refusal and a category, here bio. It is an outcome of the request, not an error to retry, and no refused prompt was sent again.

  1. Score it as planned. The rule fixed before launch gives every unanswered query the median of the shown values. A prompt that is refused therefore adds 100 predictions that are all the same number, which lowers the model's ρ on that split.
  2. Also score the answers alone. To separate how good a model's answers are from how many it gave, keep only the queries it answered, and score the model and each baseline on those same queries. A split enters this comparison only if the model answered at least 30 of its queries.
    ρanswered = ρ( yA , ŷA )A = the queries the model answered
CasePlanned scoreAnswered-only scoreWhat this case shows
Answers all 300 queries well0.500.50With no refusal the two scores are the same number
Answers 200 well, 100 refusedabout 0.380.50 on the 200The planned score drops although the answers are as good
All prompts of a split refused0.00split left outA constant prediction has no order, so ρ is 0

Made-up numbers. The baseline in an answered-only comparison is scored on the same reduced set of queries, so the comparison stays fair, but it covers fewer queries and sometimes fewer splits than the planned one.

Ridge regression on one-hot features: the baseline with no outside knowledge

Ridge regression is a fitted model: a list of weights computed from the labeled rows by one formula, then held fixed while the queries are scored. It knows nothing about proteins. It is the simplest serious baseline for this kind of data, and it is the natural counterpart to a model that has only its prompt.

  1. Encode each variant as indicators. For every sequence position that varies among the task's rows, make 21 columns, one per amino acid and one for a gap. A variant's row holds 1 in the column of the residue it has at that position and 0 elsewhere. Stacking the labeled rows gives a matrix.
    X ∈ {0, 1}k × ff = 21 v
    Row i of X is labeled variant i, and v is the number of positions that vary.
  2. Fit the weights. Find the weights that reproduce the shown values y while keeping the weights small. The penalty α sets how strongly they are held near zero. With X and y centered on their means:
    w = (X⊤X + α I)−1 X⊤ y
    Entry j of w is the estimated effect of having that residue at that position.
  3. Choose the penalty. Try 15 values of α from 0.001 to 10,000. For each, predict every labeled row from a fit on the other k − 1 rows, and keep the α with the smallest squared error. Only the labeled rows are used, so the baseline sees nothing the language model does not.
  4. Predict the queries. Encode the queries the same way and apply the weights, with the mean b of the shown values added back.
    ŷ = b + Xq wŷi = b + Σj xij wj

A protein language model: its embedding and its zero-shot score

A protein language model is a neural network trained on millions of natural protein sequences to fill in hidden residues. Its weights are fixed here: it is used as shipped. It gives two things a baseline can use. An embedding is a list of numbers computed for one sequence, a summary of how the model reads it. A zero-shot score is one number computed for one variant without any measured value, the model's own opinion of whether the substitutions look natural.

Four models are used, each pinned to a revision: ESM-2 650M, and three sizes of ESMC with about 300 million, 600 million, and 6 billion weights. All run in BF16 precision on the reserved GPU. Every one of them is used in the same three ways below, so the comparison with the language model does not rest on the choice of one protein model.

  1. Embed a sequence. The model turns a sequence of l residues into one vector per residue, the rows of H. Averaging the rows gives one vector for the sequence.
    H = PLM(sequence) ∈ ℝl × de = (1/l) Σi hi
    Row i of H is the model's state at residue i, taken from its last layer.
  2. Ridge on embeddings. Stack the labeled rows' vectors into E, scale each column to zero mean and unit spread using the labeled rows, and fit ridge exactly as in the previous entry with E in place of X.
    w = (E⊤E + α I)−1 E⊤ y
  3. Zero-shot score by masked marginals. For each position of the parent, hide that residue and ask the model for the probability of every amino acid there. A variant's score sums, over its substitutions, how much more or less likely the new residue is than the parent's.
    z = Σi ∈ substitutions [ log pi(new residue) − log pi(parent residue) ]
    No measured value enters z. Where a dataset has no single parent (Hydro, Rhomax), the score is the summed log-probability of the whole sequence instead.
  4. Ridge on one-hot features with the score appended. Add z as one more column to the one-hot matrix, scaled so that the penalty leaves it almost free. This is the augmented model of Hsu and colleagues (2022), a strong baseline when labeled rows are few.
    Xaug = [ X , 100 z ]

Controls for the embedding ridge: the same ridge on features that hold less

A ridge on a protein model's embedding can score well for two different reasons. The model may know something about the protein, or the embedding may simply be a detailed record of which residues a variant has, which any ridge could use. A feature control separates the two. It is a table with one vector per variant, built so that one specific thing is missing, and it goes through exactly the same ridge as the real embedding: the same labeled rows, the same penalty search, the same queries. Whatever the real embedding scores above a control is what the missing thing was worth.

Write a variant's sequence as s = s1 … sl, and the protein model with its trained weights as PLMθ. The real feature vector is the mean of the model's states, e = meani PLMθ(s)i. The five controls change one part of that line each.

  1. Random vector. Draw 960 numbers from a standard normal distribution, with the random seed set by the sequence itself, so the same sequence always gets the same vector and two different sequences get unrelated ones.
    r ~ N(0, I960), seeded by s
    Nothing about the sequence is in r except that it is this sequence. A ridge can memorize the labeled rows and has nothing to say about a query.
  2. Amino acid composition. Count how often each of the 20 amino acids appears and divide by the length. This is the mean of the one-hot rows of the sequence, the same averaging that makes an embedding, applied to the plainest per-residue vector there is.
    ca = (1/l) Σi [si = a]c ∈ ℝ20
    It keeps which residues a variant has and drops where they are.
  3. Untrained model. Keep the ESMC-300M architecture and replace every weight with a fresh random draw from the model's own starting distribution, θ0.
    euntrained = meani PLMθ0(s)i
    The network still turns each sequence into a vector that depends on every residue and its position, but it has learned nothing. This is the control for training itself.
  4. Shuffled sequence. Keep the trained weights and shuffle the residues of each sequence before the model reads it, with a different order σs for every sequence.
    eshuffled = meani PLMθ(σs(s))i
    The model sees the right residues in a meaningless order of their own, so only composition survives, now read through the trained model.
  5. Permuted sequence. Keep the trained weights and reorder the residues by one order σ shared by all sequences of the same length.
    epermuted = meani PLMθ(σ(s))i
    The model reads a sequence that is no protein, so its knowledge of this protein cannot apply. But two variants of one parent still differ at exactly the same places as before, so the record of what changed is intact.
Parent MKTAYI, variant A4VWhat the model reads for the parentWhat it reads for the variantPositions where the two differ
Real sequenceMKTAYIMKTVYIOne, and the sequence is a real protein
Permuted, one order for bothAYMITKVYMITKOne, and the sequence is not a protein
Shuffled, own order eachTKIMAYYVKMITNearly all: only the composition still tells them apart

A made-up six-residue example. Real sequences are 60 to 900 residues long, and one substitution changes a mean-pooled vector only slightly, which is why this detail matters.

ControlWhat the features keepWhat is missingIf it scores like the trained embedding
Random vectorNothingEverythingThe benchmark or the scoring is broken
Amino acid compositionWhich residuesPositions, and any modelThe embedding ridge was only counting residues

The comparison is between whole feature tables: each control's ridge is fit on the same 256 rows and scored on the same 300 queries as the trained embedding's ridge. The readings in the last column were written down before the controls were scored.

Trivial predictors and strata: scoring without reading the sequence

A trivial predictor is a rule that uses only an easy fact about a variant, such as how many substitutions it has. It is a control, not a contender. If a trivial predictor scores well on a split, then part of any method's score on that split can come from that easy fact, and a comparison between methods has to be read with that in mind.

  • Substitution count. Predict that a variant with more substitutions is worse: ŷ = −(number of substitutions).
  • Stratum mean. Put the labeled rows into groups, called strata, and predict each query at the mean shown value of its group. The strata are the easy fact of each dataset: the number of substitutions where there is one parent, the set of mutated positions in TrpB (which names the library a variant came from), the protein in Hydro, and clusters of near-identical sequences in Rhomax.
  • Nearest neighbor. Predict each query at the shown value of the labeled row that differs from it at the fewest positions.

The matching score is the within-stratum Spearman: compute ρ separately inside every stratum that holds at least ten queries, then average, weighting each stratum by its number of queries.

ρwithin = Σg ng ρg / Σg ng
PredictorSingle substitutions (mean value 0.8)Double substitutions (mean value 0.3)Pooled ρWithin-stratum ρ
Substitution countPredicts −1 for allPredicts −2 for allClearly positive0, because it cannot order variants inside a group
A method that reads the sequenceOrders them partly rightOrders them partly rightPositivePositive

A made-up case. Pooled rank correlation rewards knowing that doubles are worse than singles. The within-stratum score removes that reward, so it shows what a method knows beyond the group a variant belongs to.

Arms: what each version of the prompt changes, and what it tests

An arm is one version of the task. Each arm changes one thing about what a model is shown, and the queries stay the same. Comparing an arm with the plain 256-row arm isolates the effect of that one thing. The table lists every code used on this page, and where Claude Mythos 5.2 was asked it (see the two routes for why that differs by arm).

CodeWhat the model is shownWhat it testsClaude Mythos 5.2 was asked onCards
k256256 labeled rows, real residues, protein not namedThe main comparison with ridge at equal dataAll 18 splitsM1 to M4, A1
k16, k64The first 16 or 64 of the same rowsHow fast each method improves with more labeled rowsNot askedA4
klarge2,048 labeled rows, or the whole training part if it is smallerWhether a long prompt closes the gap to a baseline trained on everythingNot askedA5
k256_cipherThe same 256 rows with every amino acid renamed and every position renumberedLearning from the rows alone, with no knowledge of the protein or of chemistryThe 8 probe splitsM5
k256_shuffledThe same variants with their values dealt out at randomWhether the shown values are used at allNot askedA2
k256_flippedThe same variants with every value reflected, so the best becomes the worstWhether the model follows the shown values or its own prior beliefThe 8 probe splitsM6
k256_describedThe 256 rows plus two sentences naming the protein and the assayWhether knowing what the protein is adds anything to the rowsNot askedA3
k0_describedThe two sentences and the parent, with no labeled rowWhat the model predicts from knowledge aloneThe 8 probe splitsM7
k0_recallThe same, plus where the measurements are published, and the request to write the value the dataset reportsWhether a published value can be retrieved from memory (see memory probes)The 8 probe splitsM9

The probe splits are amylase/by_mutation, hydro/three_to_many, ired/two_to_many, nucb/two_to_many, pdz3/single_to_double, rhomax/by_wild_type, trpb/two_to_many, and fgfr2/random: one split of each dataset. Claude Fable 5.2 through the API ran every arm in the table but k0_recall on every split.

The cipher, step by step. The cipher is a relabeling of the task. It is applied to the text before the prompt is written, and it changes nothing about which variant has which value.

  1. Rename the amino acids. Draw a random one-to-one map π on the 20 letters in which no letter maps to itself, and rewrite every residue: a → π(a).
  2. Renumber the positions. Where all variants align to one parent, draw a random reordering σ of the columns and move every column: position i → σ(i). Whole-sequence datasets keep their order and get the renaming only.
  3. Write the prompt from the result. The parent, the labeled rows, and the queries are all written in the renamed and renumbered form, so the task is self-consistent.

For one-hot ridge the cipher changes nothing. Renaming and renumbering only reorder the columns of the indicator matrix, X′ = X P for a permutation matrix P, and the ridge predictions are the same for any column order:

XqP (P⊤X⊤XP + α I)−1 P⊤X⊤ y = Xq (X⊤X + α I)−1 X⊤ y

So under the cipher the language model and one-hot ridge hold exactly the same information. Whatever the model scores there is learning from the rows in front of it. Whatever it loses relative to the plain arm is what it was getting from recognizing the protein, from knowing which amino acids resemble each other, or from remembering the data.

Shuffled and flipped values. In k256_shuffled the 256 shown values are dealt out to the 256 variants at random, so the rows carry no information and any score above zero comes from elsewhere. In k256_flipped each shown value is reflected about the middle of the shown range:

y′i = min(y) + max(y) − yi

A method that learns only from the rows now ranks the queries backwards, and its ρ against the true values is the negative of its plain score. Ridge does exactly this, by its formula. A model that leans on what it already believes about the protein is pulled back toward the true order, so its flipped score sits above the negative of its plain score. The gap between the two measures the pull of prior knowledge against the evidence in the prompt.

Memory probes: has the model read these measurements before?

The FLIP2 datasets were public before the language models' training data ended, so a language model may have read them. Its score on FLIP2 can then come from three sources that must be told apart. Learning is what it takes from the labeled rows in its prompt. Knowledge is what it knows about the protein, which a protein language model also has. Memory is having read the measured values themselves. A protein language model never saw a measured value, and ridge sees only the rows it is given, so the third source is open to the language model alone. A memory probe is a test built so that one of the three sources is removed or exposed.

ProbeWhat the model getsA model that remembers the valuesA model that does notCard
Cipher (k256_cipher)256 rows with residues renamed and positions renumberedCannot use its memory: nothing can be recognizedScores the same as it would anywayM5
Data published after training (FGFR2)The same arms on a screen released on 2026-11-20Has no memory to use, so it does worse than on FLIP2 relative to ridgeStands against ridge as it does on FLIP2M3

Shuffled values (k256_shuffled)256 rows whose values are dealt to the wrong rowsStill ranks the queries wellFalls to what it knows about the proteinA2

Dataset recognitionThe parent and 30 unnamed rows, and the question of what they areNames the study or the benchmarkNames at most the protein, from its public sequenceM10
Sequence recall (API models only)The start of a parent sequence, to continueMeasures memory of the protein's sequence, not of the measurements: see the recall probeA6
Hidden residues (sequences, not measurements)A sequence with 15%, 50%, or 85% of its residues hidden, to restoreMeasures memory of the sequence, and asks whether it explains the model's accuracy: see knowing a sequenceM12

Counting exact matches, step by step. Memory of a value shows as an answer that equals it digit for digit. The count needs a yardstick, because some answers equal a value by luck.

  1. Round. Write each answer and each published value at the precision the prompts show, which is three decimals for amylase.
  2. Count. An exact match is a query whose answer equals its own published value. A near match is within 10 units of the last shown digit, which is 0.010 at three decimals.
    m = Σj [ ŷj = yj ]
  3. Deal. Keep the same answers and hand them to the queries in a random order, 2,000 times. Each deal gives a count m*. The deals show how many matches the spread of the values produces with no link between an answer and its query.
  4. Compare. Counts and deals are summed over splits, and the p-value is the share of deals that reach the real count.
    p = (1 + number of deals with m* ≥ m) / (1 + 2,000)
QueryPublished valueAnswerExactNearWhat this row shows

Q0020.0870.090noyesA close estimate: right scale, not remembered to the digit
Q0030.3110.150nonoAn ordinary wrong estimate
Q0040.0000.000yesyesA match that proves little if a third of all values are 0.000

Made-up numbers. The last row is why splits with repeating values are counted apart. In NucB the 300 test values take only three levels, and in Rhomax the value is a wavelength in whole nanometers, so a method that predicts the right level matches often without having read anything. Recall is judged on the splits whose values are continuous, where a dealt answer almost never matches: 4 of the 7 FLIP2 probe splits for Claude Mythos 5.2, and 12 of the 16 FLIP2 splits for a model that answered them all.

The comparison is between two counts over the same answers: the answers as given, and the same answers dealt at random. A method that predicts well lands near the value more often than its deal does, so the ridge baseline's own counts are shown beside the language model's.

Intervals and paired differences: how sure a comparison is

A 95% interval is a range computed from the data that says how much a score would move if a different sample of queries had been drawn. It is a statement about sampling noise in the queries. It says nothing about whether the benchmark represents other proteins.

  1. Resample the queries. For one split, draw 300 queries from its 300 with replacement, 2,000 times. Each draw is one bootstrap resample. The same 2,000 draws are used for every method on that split.
  2. Score every method on every resample. This gives 2,000 values of ρ per method and split.
  3. Average over splits. The headline number for a method is the plain mean of its ρ over the 16 FLIP2 splits, each split counting once. The same mean is taken inside each resample, which gives 2,000 values of the mean.
    m = (1/16) Σsplits ρsplit
  4. Read the interval. The interval runs from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile of the 2,000 values.
  5. Compare two methods as a pair. Because both methods are scored on the same resamples, their difference is computed inside each resample, and the interval of the difference is read from those 2,000 differences. Noise that both methods share cancels, so a difference can be sure when the two separate intervals overlap.

Where a method ran with three different draws of the labeled rows (seeds 0, 1, and 2), its score on a split is the mean of the three. Where a card reads Claude Mythos 5.2, every method on it is scored on the first 100 queries of each split, and the resamples draw 100 from those 100.

The recall probe: does a model know the parent sequence?

The recall probe is a separate, small test. It asks whether a model can continue a parent sequence from memory, which tells us whether hiding the protein's name in a prompt actually hides the protein.

  1. Cut the parent. Show the model the first 25%, 50%, or 75% of a parent sequence and ask for the next 30 residues.
  2. Score the continuation. Count the share of the 30 positions where the model's residue matches the real one.
  3. Run the control. Shuffle the parent's residues, which keeps its composition and destroys its order, and repeat. A model that only guesses common residues scores the same on both. A model that knows the sequence scores far higher on the real one.

The probe covers the six datasets with one parent, and it was run for the four API models only. It follows the logic of the continuation tests that Xinming Tu, Leo Tianlai Chen, and Sergey Ovchinnikov posted in November 2026, applied to this benchmark's own parents.

Knowing a sequence: pseudo-log-likelihood and filling in hidden residues

Whether a model knows a sequence is a separate question from whether it predicts a property of that sequence, and M12 asks if the first explains the second. Knowledge of a sequence is neither a weight of the model nor a measurement of the protein. It is a number computed for one sequence by one model, from how well the model restores residues that are hidden from it. A protein language model reports a probability for every amino acid at a hidden position, so its knowledge can be read as a pseudo-log-likelihood, PPLL for short. A general language model writes text and reports no probabilities, so its stand-in is a recovery: the share of hidden residues it writes back correctly. The recall probe above asks a model to continue a sequence from its start. This test hides residues all along the sequence and gives the same hidden positions to every model.

  1. Hide one residue and read its probability. Replace residue i of a sequence x of l residues by the mask token, run the protein language model, and read the 20 probabilities it gives at that position.
    pi = PLM(x with position i masked)i ∈ ℝ20
    Entry a of pi is the probability that residue i is amino acid a. Doing this for every position takes l passes and gives the matrix P, one row per position.
  2. Average the logs of the true residues. The PPLL is the mean, over positions, of the log-probability the model gave the residue that is really there.
    PPLL(x) = (1/l) Σi log pi(xi)
    A PPLL of 0 means the model was certain of every residue. A model that spreads its probability evenly over the 20 amino acids scores log(1/20) = −3.0. With made-up probabilities of 0.9, 0.5, and 0.05 at three positions, the logs are −0.11, −0.69, and −3.00, and the PPLL is −1.27.
  3. Hide many residues at once. Draw a set M of positions that holds 15%, 50%, or 85% of the sequence. The set is drawn once for each sequence and level and is the same for every model. A protein language model reads the sequence with every position of M masked, in one pass, and its answer at a position is its most probable amino acid there. The language model reads the sequence with an underscore at every position of M, cut into pieces of 60 residues, and writes every piece back with the underscores filled in.
    x̂i = argmaxa pi(a)orx̂i = the residue the language model wrote at i
  4. Count what came back right. The recovery at a level is the share of hidden positions where the answer equals the hidden residue. A piece that comes back at another length counts every hidden position in it as wrong.
    r = (1/|M|) Σi ∈ M [ x̂i = xi ]
    The language model's knowledge of a sequence is its recovery pooled over the three levels: every hidden position right, over every hidden position.
  5. Run two controls. A shuffled copy of a sequence keeps its residues and its length and destroys their order, so nothing but composition is left to know. The composition guess answers every hidden position with the most common residue among the visible ones. A model that only knows which amino acids are frequent scores the same as the guess, and the same on the shuffled copy as on the real sequence.
  6. Relate knowledge to error. For each rhodopsin j of the Rhomax test rows, take a model's knowledge kj and the absolute error of a prediction of its absorption maximum, in nanometers. The Spearman correlation of the two, across rhodopsins, is the result.
    aj = | ŷj − yj |ρ = Spearman(k, a)
    A negative ρ means that better-known sequences are predicted with less error. Its 95% interval comes from 2,000 resamples of the rhodopsins. The same correlation is also taken with one thing held fixed: how far a rhodopsin's true value lies from the median, since an unusual pigment could be both less known and harder to predict.

MThe hidden positions, drawn once per sequence and levelfixed|M|130 positions (39 at 15%, 222 at 85%)
PThe probabilities a protein language model gives at each position when that one position is maskedcomputedl × 20261 × 20, from 261 passes
PPLLMean log-probability of the true residuescomputedone numberone number, between −3.0 for an even guess and 0

Made-up numbers, one row for each kind of outcome.

Two comparisons are made, and their units differ. Recovery compares models on one item at a time: the same sequence with the same hidden positions, so a difference between two models at a level is a difference on identical questions. The shuffled copy receives exactly the same procedure as the real sequence, with the same length and composition, which is what makes it a fair control. Knowledge against error is a comparison across items: one point per rhodopsin, and one correlation per model. For the language model the error is that of its own prediction. For a protein language model, which predicts nothing by itself here, the error is that of the ridge on its embedding. A protein language model reads all hidden positions in one pass and does not fill them in one after another, so its recovery at 85% says what it can do from 15% of a sequence in a single reading.

Preference tuning: a generative protein language model retrained on the 256 rows

A third way to use the same 256 labeled rows is to tune a protein language model on them, and M13 runs it. Tuning is neither a ridge nor in-context learning. A ridge leaves the protein language model as it is and fits a few weights on what the model computes. In-context learning changes no weight at all. Tuning changes every weight of the protein language model, by gradient steps on a loss computed from the rows. The model here is ProGen2-small, a generative protein language model: it reads a sequence one residue at a time and gives a probability to each amino acid that could come next, where ESMC fills in residues that are hidden. Its 151,148,576 weights are fixed numbers until tuning moves them. Its score of a variant is a number computed for one sequence, which says how probable the model finds that sequence. The loss is a preference loss: it never asks the model to output a measured value, and asks only that the variant that measured higher be scored above the one that measured lower. The best-known loss of this kind is direct preference optimization, DPO.

  1. Read the sequence from both ends. A sequence x of l residues is written between the model's two end tokens, as 1, the residues, 2. Reading left to right, the model gives each residue a probability from the residues before it. The same sequence is then written backwards, and the model gives each residue a probability from the residues after it.
    ℓ→(x) = Σi log pθ(xi | x1 … xi−1)ℓ←(x) = Σi log pθ(xi | xl … xi+1)
    Each sum is a log-likelihood: one number for the whole sequence under one direction of reading. The probabilities are taken over the 25 letters of the model's vocabulary, and the closing end token is not counted, as in the scorer released with ProGen2.
  2. Average the two readings, per residue. The score is the mean log-probability of a residue, over both readings.
    sθ(x) = ( ℓ→(x) + ℓ←(x) ) / (2l)
    A score of 0 would mean the model was certain of every residue, and a model that spread its probability evenly over the 25 letters would score log(1/25) = −3.22. Because the score is a mean, a longer protein does not score lower for being longer. A PDZ3 row holds two chains: each is read by itself, and the mean is over the residues of both. With the weights as released, θ0, this is the model's zero-shot score.
  3. Set 51 rows aside. The 256 rows are divided once for each split, by a fixed seed: 205 rows to fit and 51 held out, which step 6 uses to choose. No query takes part.
  4. Compute the ranked preference loss on a batch. Take 8 of the 205 rows and sort them from the highest measured value to the lowest, so that row (1) measured highest. For each row, the ratio r says how much more probable tuning has made it than the model as released, which stays frozen.
    rj = sθ(xj) − sθ0(xj)L = −(1/b) Σk log [ exp(β r(k)) / Σm ≥ k exp(β r(m)) ]
    Term k of the loss is small when the row ranked k has a larger ratio than every row ranked below it, so the loss is lowest when the ratios follow the measured order. The weight β sets how strongly a difference in ratio counts. Rows with equal measured values are put in a random order at each step. This is the ranked form of DPO.
  5. Take a gradient step. Every weight moves a little in the direction that lowers L, by the AdamW optimizer with learning rate η. One pass over the 205 rows is an epoch of 26 steps, and a run is 20 epochs.
  6. Choose on the held-out rows. After each epoch the 51 held-out rows are scored with the weights as they then are, and the Spearman of those scores with the rows' measured values is recorded.
    h = Spearman( sθ(held-out rows), their measured values )
    Four runs start from the released weights, one for each setting of η (0.00001 or 0.0001) and β (0.1 or 2). Of their 80 epochs, the weights of the one with the highest h are kept, and called θ*.
  7. Score the queries once. Each query gets the score sθ*(x), and the order of those scores is compared with the measured values by Spearman, as for every other method. No measured value of a query is read at any earlier step.

Made-up numbers, one row for each kind of outcome.

Four more versions run beside this one on every split, and each changes one thing. The Bradley-Terry loss uses no released copy: for every two rows of a batch whose measured values differ, with row i the higher, it asks that i score above j.

LBT = mean over the pairs of log( 1 + exp( −c ( sθ(xi) − sθ(xj) ) ) )

The constant c is the mean length of the rows that fit, which turns a difference per residue back into a difference between whole sequences. A ridge on the hidden states leaves ProGen2-small as released and fits a ridge on what it computes: the last layer's vector averaged over the residues, under each reading, 2 × 1,024 numbers for a chain. It shows what the model gives without any tuning. Shuffled values are the control: the 256 measured values are dealt to the wrong rows before anything else happens, the 51 held-out rows included, and steps 3 to 7 run unchanged. Nothing then relates a sequence to its value, so this tuning can add nothing about the queries. It starts from the model as released, whose score may already rank the queries, so the control is read against that score and not against zero: shuffled values can lower it, and can raise it only by chance. A control that rose above the released model across the splits would mean that the procedure sees the queries' values somewhere. Two other batch orders repeat the chosen η and β with the rows met in another order, to show how far a score moves by that alone.

The comparison is one item against one item: the tuned model, the ridges, and the language model each rank the same queries of the same split from the same 256 rows, and two methods are compared by a paired difference. The three use the rows differently. The ridge fits on all 256 and chooses its penalty by leaving one row out at a time. The language model reads all 256 at once. Tuning fits on 205 and spends the other 51 on choosing when to stop, which a method with 151 million free weights and 205 examples needs.

Changing the tuning: one thing at a time

Each run of M14 is the tuning of the entry above with one thing changed, and two of its reads tune nothing at all. None is a new kind of method. A run is a procedure, the weights it leaves are fixed numbers once it ends, and what it gives each query is again one score. The steps below say what each change is, and the second table lists the runs by the names the tables use.

  1. Read a run after a fixed number of epochs. In the entry above the held-out rows choose the weights, θ*. A fixed recipe chooses nothing. One setting of η and β is run for E epochs, and the weights after its last step score the queries.
    θE = the weights after E epochs of one settingρE = Spearman( sθE(queries), their measured values )
    The two differ because h is a Spearman on 51 rows, which moves by about 0.1 from one draw of 51 rows to another. The epoch with the highest h is therefore partly an accident of those rows.
  2. Trace every epoch. A trace scores the queries after every epoch of every setting and keeps the scores, which gives one ρ for each of the 80 cells of the grid. Reading a trace needs the measured values of the queries, which no step of the tuning reads. A cell picked from it is therefore not a result. It says what another choice would have scored.
  3. Lower the learning rate. η = 0.000001, a tenth of the lowest rate of the grid, so that each step moves every weight about a tenth as far.
  4. Freeze the weights and add a low-rank update. Each of the model's 12 attention blocks multiplies its input by two weight matrices. A low-rank update leaves such a matrix W0 as released and adds a second path through two small matrices, A and B.
    Y = X W0 + α (X A) BA ∈ ℝdin × r, B ∈ ℝr × dout, r = 8, α = 2
    A row of X is what the layer receives for one position of a sequence, and the same row of Y is what it passes on. B starts at zero, so the model starts exactly as released. Only A and B move: 589,824 numbers over the 24 matrices, where full tuning moves 151,148,576. Whatever the rows teach must pass through the 8 numbers of X A, so this tuning cannot rewrite most of what the released model computes.
  5. Give it more rows. The first experiment also drew a larger example set for every split, up to 2,048 labeled rows. Tuning on it holds out 51 rows as before and fits on all the others. Claude Mythos 5.2 never read these larger sets, so this run is compared with the ridges fit on the same rows.
  6. Use a larger model. ProGen2-base is the same kind of model as ProGen2-small with 764,803,616 weights, five times as many.
  7. Average two rankings. Nothing is run. Each query has a rank under the tuned model and a rank under another method, and the average of the two is a new score.
    aq = ( rank1(q) + rank2(q) ) / 2
    If the average ranks the queries better than either method alone, each method holds something the other lacks. If it only matches the better of the two, the weaker one adds nothing.
  8. Score the baselines where there is no shift. A FLIP2 split draws its test queries from outside its examples, and the 51 held-out rows come from among the examples. Fitting every baseline on the same 205 rows and scoring it on the same 51 gives h for a ridge, a number that can be set beside the tuned model's h with no shift between what was learned from and what is scored.
  9. Add a likelihood term to the loss. The ranked loss L of the entry above reads only how the ratios of a batch differ from one another. It is just as low when every score of the batch falls together as when every score rises, so nothing in it holds the scores themselves, and a score is how probable the model finds a sequence. A likelihood term does hold them. Among the b sorted rows of a batch, row (k) is the preferred one of the b − k pairs it forms with the rows measured below it, and the term is the negative score of the preferred row, averaged over every pair.
    N = − Σk (b − k) sθ(x(k)) / Σk (b − k)Lλ = L + λ N
    With b = 8 there are 28 pairs: the row measured highest is the preferred one of 7 of them and the row measured lowest of none. N falls when the preferred rows become more probable, and the weight λ sets how much that counts beside the order of the ratios. At λ = 0 the loss is the one of the entry above. This is the loss of Iterative Reasoning Preference Optimization (Pang and colleagues, 2024), which adds the term for the preferred answer of each pair at λ = 1 and is the loss ProGen3 was tuned to measurements with. Weighting it over the pairs of a ranked batch is this experiment's reading of it.

Made-up numbers, with rank 3 the highest. Each method puts one query in the wrong place, a different one, and the average puts all three in the measured order.

Every run is compared as in M13: one method against one method on the same queries of the same split, by a paired difference. Two reads differ. On the held-out rows a run kept only its Spearman and not its score of each row, so there the interval comes from resampling the 16 splits and not the rows. And a fixed recipe that was picked from a trace of the first 100 queries is scored fairly only on the other queries of each split, which had no part in picking it.

Every subagent's transcript was checked for the model that answered.

M. Claude Mythos 5.2 through subagents, against controls and ESMC

Every card in this part scores Claude Mythos 5.2 and each baseline on the same queries, the first 100 of each split. No API model appears in it.

M1

With 256 examples, Claude Mythos 5.2 ties the best ridge on FLIP2

16 FLIP2 splits · first 100 queries of each · Claude Mythos 5.2 at low effort

In plain terms. Claude Mythos 5.2 reads 256 measured variants of a protein as plain text and then ranks 100 variants it has not seen. A ridge regression on a protein language model's embedding of the same variants is the standard recipe for this job. Averaged over the 16 FLIP2 splits the two rank about equally well, and neither is reliably ahead. Both are far ahead of a ridge that sees only which residues changed.

Question
Given the same 256 labeled rows, does Claude Mythos 5.2, reading them in its prompt, rank the same queries better than ridge regression on protein language model features?
Model
Claude Mythos 5.2 through fresh subagents at low effort, the level chosen on validation rows (M11). The baselines are ridge on one-hot features, ridge on the embedding of each of four protein language models, and ridge on one-hot features with each model's zero-shot score, all fit on the same 256 rows.
Data
The first prompt of each task of the 16 FLIP2 splits: 256 labeled rows drawn from the split's training part, and the first 100 of its 300 test queries. That is 1,600 queries, and every method on this card is scored on exactly those.
Steps
  1. Each prompt, 256 labeled rows and 100 queries, is written to a file, and one fresh subagent answers it.
  2. Every baseline is fit on the same 256 rows and predicts the same 100 queries.
  3. Each method's order of the queries is scored by Spearman on each split, and the 16 scores are averaged.
  4. Claude Mythos 5.2 is compared with each baseline by the paired bootstrap. The ridge it has to beat is the one with the highest mean on these same queries, a choice that favors the baselines.
Measured
The mean Spearman over the 16 splits, and its paired difference from the best ridge. The rule was set before launch: in-context learning outperforms if that difference has a 95% interval above zero.
Result
Claude Mythos 5.2 reaches a mean Spearman of 0.38 (0.33 to 0.42). The best ridge on these queries is the one on the ESMC-600M embedding, at 0.37 (0.32 to 0.41). The paired difference is +0.01 (−0.04 to +0.06), and the model's mean is the higher one in 70% of the bootstrap draws. The interval includes zero, so by the rule the result is a tie. Against three weaker baselines the interval is above zero: one-hot ridge scores 0.14 (difference +0.24 [+0.19 to +0.29]), ridge on the ESM-2 650M embedding 0.29 (+0.09 [+0.04 to +0.14]), and ridge on the ESMC-300M embedding 0.29 (+0.09 [+0.04 to +0.14]). Two more comparisons are ties: ridge on the ESMC-6B embedding at 0.35 (+0.03 [−0.02 to +0.08]), and the best zero-shot score, ESMC-6B with no label at all, at 0.35 (+0.03 [−0.01 to +0.08]). The ridges on one-hot features with a zero-shot score reach 0.36 with ESMC-600M and 0.36 with ESMC-6B.
Impact
The answer to the question on the thread is no: in-context learning does not outperform ridge regression on protein language model features. It matches it. That is still a strong result for a model with no protein-specific training and no access to an embedding. It is level with the best of four protein language models used the standard way, and above the ridges on two of them. A zero-shot score that uses no label is inside the same tie, so on these splits 256 labels buy little for any method (B1).
Limits
One prompt per split: 100 of its 300 queries, one draw of the 256 rows, and one answer per prompt. The interval covers which queries were drawn and not how much two answers to the same prompt differ. The best ridge is chosen on the queries it is scored on, which favors it. The subagent route puts a coding agent's instructions in front of every prompt (the two routes). FLIP2 was public before the model's training data ended, which cards M3, M5, M9, and M10 take up.
M2

Ahead on three splits, behind on three, and undecided on ten

16 FLIP2 splits and 2 FGFR2 splits · first 100 queries of each · Claude Mythos 5.2 at low effort

In plain terms. The tie of M1 is not sixteen near-draws. On a few splits the language model is far ahead, on a few it is far behind, and on most of them 100 queries cannot tell the two methods apart. Its largest lead is on the rhodopsin dataset, Rhomax. Its largest deficit is on a split that asks it to rank variants more stable than any it was shown.

Question
On which splits is Claude Mythos 5.2 ahead of the best ridge, on which is it behind, and is the mean of card M1 carried by a few of them?
Model
As in M1: Claude Mythos 5.2 at low effort, and the ridge with the highest mean on the same queries.
Data
The same prompts as M1, read one split at a time, and the two FGFR2 splits of card M3.
Steps
  1. For each split, take the Spearman of each method on its 100 queries.
  2. Take the paired difference and its 95% interval from the same 2,000 resamples.
  3. Call a split decided when the interval excludes zero.
Measured
The difference in Spearman on each split, and how many splits are decided each way.
Result
Against the ridge on the ESMC-600M embedding: 3 of 16 ahead, 3 behind, 10 undecided. Ahead: rhomax/by_wild_type (+0.53 [+0.29 to +0.75]), amylase/close_to_far (+0.45 [+0.20 to +0.68]), and amylase/one_to_many (+0.24 [+0.05 to +0.42]). Behind: hydro/low_to_high (−0.56 [−0.80 to −0.30]), trpb/by_position (−0.21 [−0.40 to −0.04]), and hydro/three_to_many (−0.17 [−0.32 to −0.02]). On hydro/low_to_high the model's Spearman is negative, −0.26, where the ridge scores 0.30. Against the same ridge on the two FGFR2 splits the differences are +0.17 (+0.03 to +0.32) and +0.16 (−0.05 to +0.37), and card M3 compares with the ridge that is best there. Leaving Rhomax out, a check added after the results were seen, the 15 other splits give 0.36 for the model and 0.38 for the same ridge, a difference of −0.02 (−0.07 to +0.03). Against the ridge that is best on those 15 splits, on one-hot features with the ESMC-6B score, the difference is −0.03 (−0.07 to +0.01).
Impact
No method wins everywhere, so which one to use depends on the split. The model's lead on Rhomax comes from knowledge it already holds (M8, M9), and with that dataset set aside the tie stays a tie and leans to the ridge. The failure on hydro/low_to_high is the opposite case: every test value lies above the highest value among the examples, and the model ranks those variants in the wrong order.
Limits
With 100 queries a single split's interval is wide, so a split that is not decided may still differ. Sixteen intervals at 95% are expected to exclude zero by chance about once when nothing differs.
M3

On data published after training, Claude Mythos 5.2 again ties the best ridge

FGFR2, MaveDB score set urn:mavedb:00001329-a-3, published 2026-11-20 · 2 splits · first 100 queries of each

In plain terms. FLIP2 was on the internet before these models were trained, so a good score there could come from having read the answers. This dataset was published in November 2026, and the models' training data end in June 2026. On it the language model does as well as the best ridge, the same outcome as on FLIP2.

Question
Does the comparison come out the same on measurements published after the model's training data ended, which it cannot have read?
Model
As in M1.
Data
A drug-resistance screen of the FGFR2 kinase domain: 1,876 single amino acid changes, each with the base-2 logarithm of its mean score, published on MaveDB on 2026-11-20. The models' training data end in June 2026. The changes are divided at random (fgfr2/random) and by position (fgfr2/by_position).
Steps
  1. Build tasks from the two splits exactly as for FLIP2: 256 labeled rows and the first 100 queries.
  2. Ask Claude Mythos 5.2 and fit every baseline on the same rows.
  3. Score each split, and compare each method with the others by the paired bootstrap.
Measured
Spearman on each of the two splits, and the paired difference between Claude Mythos 5.2 and the best ridge over the two.
Result
Over the two FGFR2 splits Claude Mythos 5.2 reaches 0.56 (0.46 to 0.65). The best ridge there, on one-hot features with the ESMC-6B score, reaches 0.57 (0.47 to 0.66), and the paired difference is −0.01 (−0.11 to +0.09). On fgfr2/random the model scores 0.66 and that ridge 0.70. On fgfr2/by_position they score 0.46 and 0.44. The model is above the ridge on the ESMC-600M embedding (0.40, difference +0.16 [+0.04 to +0.29]) and above one-hot ridge (0.30, difference +0.27 [+0.13 to +0.40]). The zero-shot score of ESMC-6B alone is 0.48 (difference +0.08 [−0.05 to +0.21]). These 100 queries are easier than the rest for every method: on all 300 queries of each split the same ridge scores 0.45 and the zero-shot score of ESMC-6B 0.40. The methods are compared on the same queries, so the comparison stands, but the scores on this card are not the level of the dataset.
Impact
The tie on FLIP2 is not explained by the model having read FLIP2's values. On measurements it cannot have seen it is level with the best ridge, and above the embedding ridge that was best on FLIP2. What the model keeps here is its knowledge of the protein, and FGFR2 is a well-studied human kinase.
Limits
One protein, two splits, and 100 queries each. FGFR2 is a well-studied human kinase, and the model names it from its sequence (M10), so this dataset removes memory of the measurements and keeps knowledge of the protein. The date is MaveDB's publication date, and an earlier preprint of the same screen cannot be ruled out from it.
M4

On FLIP2, the average of the model's ranking and the ridge's beats both

16 FLIP2 splits · first 100 queries of each · Claude Mythos 5.2 and the best ridge, ranks averaged

In plain terms. If two methods are equally good for the same reasons, combining them gains nothing. If they are good for different reasons, their errors partly cancel. Giving each query the average of its two ranks scores higher than either method alone. So the language model and the ridge on a protein language model know different things.

Question
Do the language model and the best ridge make the same mistakes, or does averaging their rankings beat both?
Model
Claude Mythos 5.2 at low effort and the best ridge on the same queries.
Data
The 16 FLIP2 splits, first 100 queries of each.
Steps
  1. Rank the 100 queries of a split by each method.
  2. Give each query the mean of its two ranks.
  3. Score that combined order like any other method.
Measured
Mean Spearman of the combined order, and its paired difference from each method alone.
Result
The averaged ranking reaches 0.44 (0.40 to 0.48), which is +0.06 (+0.03 to +0.09) above Claude Mythos 5.2 alone and +0.08 (+0.05 to +0.10) above the ridge alone. On the two FGFR2 splits it reaches 0.61, which is +0.05 (0.00 to +0.10) above the model and +0.04 (−0.02 to +0.10) above the ridge, with intervals that reach zero.
Impact
The practical answer to the thread is neither method alone. The two tie on average and disagree split by split (M2), and an average of their rankings with nothing to tune has the highest mean on this page. A lab with a few hundred labels and a ridge already fitted gains from asking the language model as well.
Limits
The average uses equal weights and no tuning. It was fixed before launch and is applied unchanged.
M5

Enciphering the residues costs Claude Mythos 5.2 nearly half of its score

7 FLIP2 probe splits · first 100 queries of each · arm k256_cipher

In plain terms. The cipher renames every amino acid and renumbers every position. The prompt still holds everything a one-hot ridge uses, and nothing that identifies the protein. The model's score falls by nearly half, and what is left is close to what one-hot ridge gets from the same rows.

Question
With every amino acid renamed and every position renumbered, so that nothing about the protein can be recognized, how much of the language model's score remains?
Model
Claude Mythos 5.2 at low effort. One-hot ridge is the reference, because the cipher leaves its predictions unchanged.
Data
The 7 FLIP2 probe splits, one per dataset, with the same 256 rows and the same first 100 queries as the plain arm.
Steps
  1. Apply the cipher to the parent, the labeled rows, and the queries of a plain prompt.
  2. Ask a fresh subagent, and score its answers against the true values.
  3. Compare with the plain arm of the same splits, and with one-hot ridge, as paired differences.
Measured
Mean Spearman under the cipher, its paired difference from the plain arm, and its paired difference from one-hot ridge on the same rows.
Result
On the 7 FLIP2 probe splits the plain prompt scores 0.50 (0.43 to 0.55) and the enciphered one 0.28 (0.20 to 0.35). The plain prompt is +0.22 (+0.16 to +0.28) above the enciphered one. One-hot ridge on the same rows scores 0.21. The enciphered model is +0.07 (0.00 to +0.13) from it, an interval whose lower end is at zero, and −0.15 (−0.22 to −0.07) from the best ridge. On fgfr2/random the enciphered prompt scores 0.34, where the plain prompt scores 0.66 and one-hot ridge 0.46.
Impact
Nearly half of the model's score needs the protein to be recognizable, and that part is what puts it level with a ridge on a protein language model. With the protein hidden it is still a competent learner from 256 anonymous rows, about as good as one-hot ridge, which shows that it reads the rows and does not only recite. The drop is very uneven across datasets (M8): on Rhomax the cipher removes the whole score.
Limits
The cipher removes three things at once: recognition of the protein, knowledge of which amino acids resemble each other, and any remembered value. The drop from the plain arm is their sum and cannot be divided among them here. Seven splits and 700 queries.
M6

Reversed values reverse the model's ranking on every dataset but two

7 FLIP2 probe splits · first 100 queries of each · arm k256_flipped

In plain terms. Every shown value is reflected, so the best variants are shown as the worst. A method that learns only from the rows would then rank the queries exactly backwards. On six of the eight datasets the model does rank them backwards, most of the way. So the rows in its prompt, and not remembered answers, drive its ranking there. On Rhomax it keeps the true order against the rows.

Question
When every shown value is reflected, so the best variant is shown as the worst, does the model follow the rows in front of it or what it already believes about the protein?
Model
Claude Mythos 5.2 at low effort.
Data
The same 256 rows and queries as the plain arm, with each shown value reflected about the middle of the shown range. The answers are scored against the true, unreflected values.
Steps
  1. Reflect the shown values and write the prompt.
  2. Ask the model, and score its answers against the true values.
  3. Compare with the negative of its plain score, which is what a method that learns only from the rows would get.
Measured
Mean Spearman against the true values under reflected rows. A value near the negative of the plain score means the model follows its prompt. A value that stays positive means it answers from what it already holds.
Result
On the 7 FLIP2 probe splits Claude Mythos 5.2 scores −0.24 (−0.30 to −0.17) against the true values, where its plain score is 0.50 and a pure learner from the rows would score the negative of that. On fgfr2/random it scores −0.49 against a plain 0.66. By dataset (the table of M8) the score under reversed rows is negative on six of the eight probe splits, near zero on ired/two_to_many (0.05), and still positive on rhomax/by_wild_type (0.58).
Impact
Where the ranking reverses, the model is doing what the thread asked about: learning the relation between sequence and value from the examples in its context. That includes FGFR2, which it cannot have read. A reversed ranking also rules out that the plain score on those datasets is recited, because a recited ranking would not turn around. Rhomax is the opposite case, and card M9 looks at it.
Limits
A score between the two extremes mixes following the rows with prior belief and does not say which belief: general knowledge of the protein or memory of its measurements. The figure is the first one of card M5.
M7

With no examples, Claude Mythos 5.2 matches the zero-shot score of a protein language model on FLIP2

7 FLIP2 probe splits · first 100 queries of each · arm k0_described

In plain terms. Told only which protein and which assay, and shown no measurement, the model still ranks the variants. A protein language model does the same job with its zero-shot score, which also uses no label. On the seven FLIP2 probe splits the two are level. This is the knowledge the model brings before it reads a single row.

Question
With the protein and the assay named and no labeled row, how well does the language model rank the queries, beside the zero-shot scores of the protein language models, which also see no label?
Model
Claude Mythos 5.2 at low effort. The reference is each protein language model's zero-shot score.
Data
The same queries as the plain arm. The prompt holds two sentences that name the protein and the assay, the parent where there is one, and the queries.
Steps
  1. Write the prompt with no measured row.
  2. Ask the model and score its answers.
  3. Compare with each zero-shot score on the same queries, as a paired difference.
Measured
Mean Spearman with no examples, and its paired difference from the best zero-shot score on the same queries.
Result
On the 7 FLIP2 probe splits Claude Mythos 5.2 with no examples scores 0.39 (0.32 to 0.45). The zero-shot scores on the same queries are 0.32 for ESMC-6B, 0.31 for ESMC-600M, 0.26 for ESM-2 650M, and 0.26 for ESMC-300M. The paired difference from the best of them is +0.07 (0.00 to +0.15), with its lower end at zero. The 256 rows add +0.10 (+0.04 to +0.17) to the model's score with no examples. Without Rhomax, a check added afterward, the model scores 0.35 and the best zero-shot score on those six splits, ESMC-600M, 0.34, a difference of 0.00 (−0.07 to +0.07). On fgfr2/random the model scores 0.38 and ESMC-6B 0.52.
Impact
Before it reads any example, the model already carries about as much usable knowledge of these proteins as a protein language model's likelihoods do. That explains why 256 rows are enough for it to tie a ridge built on those models.
Limits
A language model with no examples can draw on general knowledge of the protein and on anything it remembers of the measurements, and this arm cannot tell them apart. Card M9 asks for the remembered values directly.
M8

Only Rhomax shows all three signs of an answer from prior knowledge

The 8 probe splits, one per dataset · first 100 queries of each · four versions of the prompt

In plain terms. The means of cards M5, M6, and M7 hide that the eight datasets behave differently. On four of them the 256 rows clearly add to what the model knew beforehand, and reversing the rows reverses its ranking. On three it does about as well with no rows as with them. On one, Rhomax, every sign says the answer comes from what the model already knew: it scores nearly as well with no examples, it keeps the true order when the rows are reversed, and it loses everything when the residues are enciphered.
