Question
Is the mix of learning from the rows and prior knowledge the same in every dataset, or does the mean of cards M5, M6, and M7 hide datasets that work differently?
Model
Claude Mythos 5.2 at low effort, and the ridge on the ESMC-600M embedding, which is the best ridge on FLIP2 (M1).
Data
The 8 probe splits, first 100 queries of each, under the plain, no-examples, enciphered, and reversed prompts.
Steps
  1. Take the Spearman of each version of the prompt on each split.
  2. Read three signs for each dataset: how much the 256 rows add to the score with no examples, whether the cipher removes the score, and whether reversed rows reverse the ranking.
Measured
Spearman on 100 queries per split and version. A dataset is answered from prior knowledge if the score with no examples is close to the plain score, the cipher removes it, and reversed rows do not reverse it.
Result
The table gives every cell. On trpb/two_to_many, fgfr2/random, hydro/three_to_many, and amylase/by_mutation the plain prompt scores well above the prompt with no examples, and the reversed prompt scores well below zero. On pdz3/single_to_double the model scores the same with and without rows, yet it keeps most of that score under the cipher and reverses under reversed rows, so it can reach the answer either way. On nucb/two_to_many and ired/two_to_many the rows add nothing to the score with no examples. On rhomax/by_wild_type the model scores 0.66 with no examples and 0.74 with 256. Under the cipher it falls to −0.02, and under reversed rows it stays at 0.58. The ridge on the same rows scores 0.21.
Impact
The model's largest lead over the ridge in M2 is on the one dataset that it answers from prior knowledge, so that lead is not evidence of in-context learning. Rhomax pairs rhodopsins from many organisms with their absorption maxima, and its split holds out whole families of sequences. That is hard for a ridge and easy for a reader of the rhodopsin literature, where absorption maxima are reported protein by protein. On the other datasets the cipher and the reversal show a model that reads its rows. A benchmark meant to measure in-context learning in a language model needs datasets like FGFR2, published after the model was trained.
Limits
This reading by dataset was added after the results were seen, and it rests on 100 queries and one answer per cell, so differences of 0.1 between cells are within noise. One split stands for each dataset.
M9

Claude Mythos 5.2 does not write out FLIP2's continuous values, and on Rhomax it gives wavelengths to the nanometer

FLIP2 probe splits and fgfr2/random · first 100 queries of each · arm k0_recall and exact matches

In plain terms. If the model had memorized a dataset's table, then asked for the published value of each test variant it would write some of them exactly. On the four datasets with continuous values it wrote none of 400. On Rhomax, whose values are whole nanometers, it gave the exact wavelength for about one query in ten and came within 10 nm for more than half, with no example in its prompt. Whether that is recall of published values or accurate knowledge of each rhodopsin, it is not learned from the prompt.

Question
Asked outright for the value a named dataset reports for each test variant, can Claude Mythos 5.2 write it down?
Model
Claude Mythos 5.2 at low effort. The best ridge's own matches under 256 examples are the reference for what good prediction alone gives.
Data
The 7 FLIP2 probe splits and fgfr2/random, where no value can have been read. 4 of the seven have continuous values. The other 3 (amylase/by_mutation, nucb/two_to_many, and rhomax/by_wild_type) have few distinct values, so an answer can equal a published value by chance, and each is read beside its own deal. The prompt names the protein, the assay, and where the measurements are published, and shows no measured row.
Steps
  1. Ask for the reported value of each of the 100 queries.
  2. Count the answers that equal their query's published value, and those near it.
  3. Deal the same answers to the queries at random 2,000 times, and count again.
  4. Also compare the order of the answers with the arm that asks for a score and no published value.
Measured
Exact and near matches against the dealt counts, with the share of deals that reach the real count as a p-value. Recall of the values is called at p below 0.01 on the continuous splits, a rule fixed before any answer. Reading the splits with few distinct values one at a time, and Rhomax under every version of the prompt, was added after the answers were seen.
Result
On the 4 FLIP2 probe splits with continuous values, the answers to the request for published values match 0 of 400 exactly, where a random deal of the same answers matches 0.1. They match 4 of 400 nearly, where the deal matches 3.4 (p = 0.450). By the rule fixed beforehand, no recall of values is shown. With 256 examples the model matches 1 of 400 exactly and the best ridge 3 of 400. On fgfr2/random, where recall is impossible, it matches 0 of 100. Asking for published values did not improve the ranking over asking for a score: 0.33 against 0.39 (difference −0.06 [−0.09 to −0.03]). Rhomax, read by itself afterward, has exact matches of 7 of 100 (dealt 0.9) with the protein named and no examples, 11 of 100 (dealt 1.1) when published values are asked for, 14 of 100 (dealt 1.2) with 256 examples, 11 of 100 (dealt 1.4) with reversed rows, and 4 of 100 (dealt 1.2) under the cipher. The best ridge has 1 of 100 (dealt 0.7). Answers within 10 nm number 54 of 100 (dealt 20.0) with no examples and 27 of 100 (dealt 23.5) under the cipher. NucB has three activity levels, so its 55 of 100 (dealt 43.7) says nothing about memory.
Impact
The scores on FLIP2's continuous datasets are not produced by reciting their tables, which answers the thread's worry for most of the benchmark. That does not make FLIP2 unseen data: the model has read about every one of these datasets (M10), and on Rhomax its answers do not depend on the rows in its prompt. For this model, a score on Rhomax should not be read as in-context learning.
Limits
A model that holds values and declines to write them, or holds them only as a rough order, passes this test. So the test bounds recall of exact numbers and nothing wider. On a whole-number scale such as Rhomax's nanometers, an accurate predictor also lands on the exact value at times, so the Rhomax counts do not separate recall of a published table from accurate knowledge of each protein. One prompt per split, and the low effort level.
M10

Claude Mythos 5.2 names the source study of all seven FLIP2 datasets from 30 unlabeled rows

8 datasets · the parent and 30 unnamed rows of each · Claude Mythos 5.2 at low effort

In plain terms. Each dataset's parent sequence and 30 measured rows were shown with no name on them, and the model was asked what they were. For every FLIP2 dataset it named the protein, the kind of measurement, and the study that the benchmark took the data from. For FGFR2, published after its training data end, it named the protein from its sequence and said that the source was unknown.

Question
Shown a parent sequence and 30 measured rows with no name attached, does the model know which protein, which measurement, and which study they are?
Model
Claude Mythos 5.2 at low effort, one fresh subagent per dataset.
Data
For each of the eight datasets, the parent and the first 30 labeled rows of a plain prompt of its probe split, followed by the question. The prompt names nothing.
Steps
  1. Ask: which protein do these measurements describe, what was measured, and in which study or dataset were they published?
  2. Read the three-line answer against the source that the FLIP2 site lists for the dataset, as read on 2026-11-22.
  3. Mark protein, measurement, and source as named or not.
Measured
Three marks per dataset. Naming the protein is knowledge of a public sequence. Naming the study is recognition of the dataset.
Result
All seven FLIP2 datasets: protein named, measurement named, and source study named, as the table lists. FGFR2: the kinase domain named from its sequence, and the assay and the source both given as “unknown”.
Impact
FLIP2 is not unseen data for this model. It knows that these studies exist and what they measured. That is recognition of the datasets and does not show that it holds their values (M9). It does mean that FLIP2 alone cannot separate in-context learning from prior knowledge, so the controls of part B and the FGFR2 dataset carry that weight. The FGFR2 answer is what a dataset from after the cutoff should give: the protein is known and the study is not.
Limits
One answer per dataset, marked by the author of this page and not by a second reader. Recognizing a study is not the same as remembering its numbers, which is what M9 tests. Several answers hedge with “most likely”, and a named source was marked right if it is the study the benchmark lists.
M11

High effort did not reliably beat low effort

3 validation prompts at four effort levels · 7 FLIP2 probe splits at low and at high effort

In plain terms. The model can be told to think more before it answers, which costs tokens and time. On three validation prompts the levels low, medium, and high scored the same to within a hundredth, so the rule chose low. On test rows high effort was a little higher on average, inside the noise, and it took more than twice the thinking.

EffortValidation prompts answeredMean Spearman on themMedian thinking tokens a promptMedian seconds a prompt

Extra high2 of 3not averaged8,12079
Maximum0 of 3no answer
Question
Does Claude Mythos 5.2 rank variants better when it is told to think harder before answering?
Model
Claude Mythos 5.2 through fresh subagents at low, medium, high, and extra high effort. The level each subagent ran at was read from its transcript.
Data
Three validation prompts (amylase/by_mutation, hydro/three_to_many, ired/two_to_many), 100 queries each, at every level. On test rows, the plain 256-row prompt of the 7 FLIP2 probe splits and fgfr2/random at low and at high effort.
Steps
  1. Ask the three validation prompts at each level, and average each level's three scores.
  2. Choose the lowest level within 0.02 of the best mean.
  3. Ask the test prompts of the probe splits at high effort as well, and compare with low effort on the same queries.
Measured
Mean validation Spearman by level, the paired difference between high and low effort on test rows, and what each level spent in thinking tokens and in seconds.
Result
Validation means over three prompts are 0.580 at low, 0.575 at medium, and 0.581 at high effort, and the rule chose low. Extra high answered 2 of the three prompts (0.678 and 0.297), and maximum none. On test rows of the 7 FLIP2 probe splits high effort scores 0.52 (0.46 to 0.58) and low effort 0.50 (0.43 to 0.55), a paired difference of +0.03 (−0.01 to +0.07). The gain is on two splits: Rhomax (0.89 against 0.74) and NucB (0.44 against 0.34). On fgfr2/random high effort is lower (0.60 against 0.66). Against the best ridge on these seven splits, low effort is +0.07 (+0.01 to +0.13) and high effort +0.10 (+0.04 to +0.15). The seven include Rhomax, and without it, a check added afterward, the six other splits give 0.46 at low effort, 0.46 at high effort, and 0.46 for the ridge. A test prompt took a median of 2,156 thinking tokens and 29 s at low effort, and 5,567 and 53 s at high effort.
Impact
For this task the cheapest setting is enough. The ranking seems to be available to the model without long deliberation, and what high effort gained is concentrated on Rhomax, the dataset that it answers from prior knowledge. High effort was not asked on all 16 splits, so the page cannot give M1 at high effort. The difference between the two levels on the probe splits is smaller than the interval of M1.
Limits
Three validation prompts cannot tell levels apart more finely than a few hundredths. Extra high answered two of its three prompts before the account's usage limit stopped it, and maximum returned nothing in ten minutes a prompt, so neither was scored on test rows. High effort ran on 8 test prompts and low on 18.
M12

Claude Mythos 5.2 can write most of these proteins out, and whether it can does not predict how well it predicts them

A second experiment, run on 23 November 2026 · 48 Rhomax test rows, 6 dataset parents, and 12 shuffled copies · Claude Mythos 5.2 at low effort and four protein language models

In plain terms. A model might score well on a protein simply because it knows that protein well. To test this, residues were hidden in 66 sequences and each model was asked to restore them. Claude Mythos 5.2 restores most rhodopsins nearly whole, even with 85% of the residues hidden, which no protein language model does. But its error on a rhodopsin's absorption maximum is the same whether or not it could write that rhodopsin out. For the protein language models, how well a model knows a sequence predicts the error of the ridge on its embedding for one model of four.

A negative correlation means that better-known sequences are predicted with less error. The median error is over all 100 rhodopsins the model answered. The one-hot ridge's is 22.1 nm.

Question
Does how well a model knows a protein sequence predict how well it predicts that protein's property?
Model
Claude Mythos 5.2 at low effort, one fresh subagent per prompt, and ESM-2 650M, ESMC-300M, ESMC-600M, and ESMC-6B at their pinned revisions.
Data
118 sequences: the parents of the six datasets that have one (amylase, IRED, NucB, TrpB, PDZ3, FGFR2), the 100 Rhomax test rows that Claude Mythos 5.2 answered, and shuffled copies of the 6 parents and of 6 rhodopsins. Rhomax is the one dataset in which every test row is its own natural sequence with its own measured value, so it is the one place the question can be asked sequence by sequence. The language model read 66 of the 118: the parents, 48 rhodopsins drawn with a fixed seed, and the 12 shuffled copies.
Steps
  1. For each sequence, draw the positions to hide at 15%, 50%, and 85%, once, for every model (the primer).
  2. Run each protein language model on all 118 sequences: its PPLL with one position masked at a time, and its recovery at each level with all the hidden positions masked in one pass.
  3. Ask Claude Mythos 5.2 in six prompts of 33 sequences. Each sequence meets each level once, in three different prompts, so no prompt shows a residue that the same prompt hides at another level.
  4. Check every subagent's transcript: the model that answered, its effort level, and that it read its prompt and wrote its answer and did nothing else.
  5. For each rhodopsin, take the absolute error of the absorption maximum that each method predicted in the cards above: the language model with no examples and with 256, and the ridge on each embedding fit on 256 rows.
  6. Correlate knowledge with error across the rhodopsins, with an interval from 2,000 resamples, and repeat with how unusual the true value is held fixed.
Measured
Recovery by model, kind of sequence, and level. The Spearman of knowledge with absolute error across rhodopsins, where a relation counts as present when its 95% interval excludes zero. That rule, the sequences, and the levels were fixed before any answer was read.
Result
Claude Mythos 5.2 restores 91%, 76%, and 57% of the hidden residues of the rhodopsins at 15%, 50%, and 85% hidden. ESMC-6B, the best protein language model, restores 59%, 54%, and 12%, and the composition guess 11%, 11%, and 10%. On shuffled copies every model is at the composition guess, so nothing is restored from composition. The language model's answers are whole or a guess: 34, 32, and 23 of the 48 rhodopsins came back at least 90% right at the three levels, and 19 at all three. No protein language model reached 90% on any rhodopsin at any level. Of the parents, FGFR2 came back at 100% and TrpB at 100% with half the residues hidden, amylase at 100% and PDZ3 at 100% with 15% hidden, and none above 18% at 85%. Across the rhodopsins, the Spearman of the model's recovery with its absolute error is −0.15 (−0.41 to +0.13) with no examples and −0.04 (−0.33 to +0.24) with 256 examples. Both intervals hold zero, so by the rule set beforehand no relation is shown. For the protein language models the PPLL against the error of the ridge on the same model's embedding gives −0.50 (−0.64 to −0.33) for ESMC-600M and −0.20 (−0.35 to −0.02) for ESM-2 650M, a relation by the same rule, and −0.08 (−0.30 to +0.15) for ESMC-300M and +0.03 (−0.18 to +0.25) for ESMC-6B, none. Read after the results were seen: the 8 rhodopsins that came back whole at no level have a median error of 3.5 nm with no examples, and the 19 that came back whole at every level 4.0 nm. The three ESMC models rank the rhodopsins by PPLL nearly alike (Spearman 0.82 to 0.95 between them), so the ESMC-600M relation belongs to that model's ridge and not to which sequences are well known.
Impact
The model's accuracy on Rhomax (M8, M9) is not explained by having each test sequence memorized: it predicts the rhodopsins it could not write out as well as the ones it could. Knowing a sequence and predicting its property are separate abilities in this range. The result also sharpens M3: the FGFR2 screen is new to the model, and the FGFR2 kinase domain is not, since it writes the domain out with half of it hidden. For the protein language models, a sequence's PPLL is not a usable warning of where a ridge on the embedding will fail: the relation appears for one model and is absent for the largest.
Limits
One dataset, one split, and one property. The rhodopsins include variants of shared wild types, so they are not independent and the intervals are too narrow by an unknown amount. Forty-eight sequences detect a correlation of about 0.4 or more, so a weak relation for the language model is not excluded. Each prompt was asked once, and whether a sequence came back whole was not steady across levels: amylase came back whole at 15% hidden and as a guess at 50%. The property prompts show a whole sequence and these prompts hide at least 15% of it, so a sequence the model failed to restore may still be one it recognizes when whole. Ten correlations were tested with no correction. The test does not separate knowledge of the rhodopsin family from memory of measured wavelengths, which is what M9 speaks to.
M13

Question
Given the same 256 labeled rows, does a generative protein language model that is tuned on them with a preference loss rank the same queries better than Claude Mythos 5.2 reading them in its prompt, and better than the best ridge on ESMC features?
Model
ProGen2-small, 151 million weights, from a pinned copy of the released weights that was checked against its authors' reference score before use. Every weight is tuned. Claude Mythos 5.2 and the ridges are those of M1 and M3: no model was asked again and no ridge was fit again.
Data
The tasks of M1 and M3, unchanged: for each of the 16 FLIP2 splits and the 2 FGFR2 splits, the 256 labeled rows of the first draw and the first 100 test queries, 1,800 queries in all. Tuning divides the 256 rows into 205 to fit and 51 held out.
Steps
  1. Score the queries with ProGen2-small as released, which is its score with no examples, and fit a ridge on its hidden states on the 256 rows.
  2. Tune the model with the ranked preference loss under each of four settings for 20 epochs, read the Spearman on the held-out rows after every epoch, and keep the weights of the best epoch (the primer).
  3. Do the same with the Bradley-Terry loss, with the ranked loss on shuffled values, and with the ranked loss under two other batch orders.
  4. Score the queries once with each kept set of weights. No measured value of a query is read before that.
  5. Compare each version with Claude Mythos 5.2 and with the best ridge by the paired bootstrap, on the same queries.
Measured
The mean Spearman over the 16 FLIP2 splits, and over the 2 FGFR2 splits apart, and the paired difference of the tuned model from Claude Mythos 5.2 and from the best ridge. The loss, the four settings, the choice on held-out rows, and the rule were fixed before any ProGen2 score was computed: a difference whose 95% interval excludes zero is a win or a loss, and one that includes it is a tie. The control is read first: over the splits, tuning on shuffled values must not score above the model as released. That reading was set after the two pilot splits were scored and before the other 16 were read. The plan had said the control must score near zero, which holds only where the released model ranks nothing.
Result
The control passes. Tuned on shuffled values the model scores 0.13 (0.08 to 0.18) on FLIP2, and its difference from the released model's score is −0.11 (−0.16 to −0.05), an interval below zero. Tuning on the measured values scores +0.13 (+0.07 to +0.20) above tuning on shuffled ones. The tuned model is behind both methods. With the ranked preference loss it reaches 0.26 (0.21 to 0.31), where Claude Mythos 5.2 reaches 0.38 (0.33 to 0.42) and the best ridge 0.37 (0.32 to 0.41). The paired differences are −0.12 (−0.16 to −0.07) from the language model and −0.10 (−0.16 to −0.05) from the ridge. Both intervals lie below zero, so by the rule the tuned model loses to each. The two other batch orders give 0.27 and 0.26. Split by split against the language model: 1 of 16 ahead, 7 behind, 8 undecided. Against the ridge: 1 of 16 ahead, 5 behind, 10 undecided. Tuning does not improve on the released model here. ProGen2-small with no examples scores 0.24 (0.19 to 0.29), and the tuned model differs from it by +0.02 (−0.04 to +0.08) with the ranked loss and by 0.00 (−0.06 to +0.05) with the Bradley-Terry loss, two ties. The ridge on its hidden states scores 0.19. The released model is itself −0.10 (−0.14 to −0.06) from the score ESMC-600M gives with no examples, and the tuned model stays below that score (−0.08 [−0.13 to −0.02]) and above the one-hot ridge (+0.12 [+0.07 to +0.18]). The tuning did learn the rows. On the 51 held-out rows the mean Spearman over the FLIP2 splits rises from 0.24 for the released model to 0.63 at the chosen checkpoint. Part of that rise is the choice among 80 checkpoints, since the control reaches 0.20 on its own shuffled held-out rows by the same choice. The lower learning rate was chosen on 13 of 16 splits and the larger weight on 12 of 16. Where it gains and where it loses. Against its own score with no examples, tuning gains most on pdz3/single_to_double (−0.05 to 0.44) and on amylase/by_mutation (0.35 to 0.63), where the test variants are mutated at positions the examples also mutate. It loses most on hydro/low_to_high (0.31 to −0.20), where every test value lies above the examples' values, and on amylase/close_to_far (0.29 to 0.01), where the test variants are mutated at positions no example touches. On FGFR2 the tuned model scores 0.31 (0.19 to 0.43), which is −0.25 (−0.39 to −0.12) from the language model and −0.26 (−0.40 to −0.11) from the best ridge there. On all 300 queries of each split, where only the ridges can be compared, it scores 0.26 (0.23 to 0.28) on FLIP2 against 0.36 (0.33 to 0.38) for the best ridge on those queries (−0.10 [−0.13 to −0.07]). On all FGFR2 queries the tuned models tie the best ridge, at 0.38 with the ranked loss and 0.45 with the Bradley-Terry loss against 0.46 (−0.08 [−0.16 to +0.01] and −0.01 [−0.07 to +0.06]).
Impact
The question behind this card was whether the tie of M1 is a tie with a weak baseline, since a ridge never changes its protein model and preference tuning changes every weight. Under the recipe set in advance the tuned generative model is behind the ridge and behind the language model, and it does not improve on its own score with no examples. The control says how that comes about. The measured values add about as much (the +0.13 over shuffled values) as moving every weight takes away from the released model's ranking (the −0.11 of the control). The tuning does learn rows like its examples, as the held-out rows show, and under this recipe that gain does not reach test queries that FLIP2 draws from outside the examples. M14 finds the reason in the recipe and not in the method: the held-out rows choose a worse setting and stopping point than one setting run to a fixed length, and with that fixed recipe the tuned model is level with the ridge and with the language model. So the ridge is not a weak baseline. The method that changes every weight gets level with it at best.
Limits
One model, the smallest ProGen2, with 151 million weights, one grid of four settings, and one way of choosing a checkpoint. M14 changes each in turn. The released model starts below ESMC-600M on these queries, so the card compares recipes on different protein models and does not separate the tuning from the model that is tuned. The setting and the epoch are chosen on 51 rows drawn from the same part of a split as the rows the model is fit on, so the choice cannot see the shift that the test queries bring. One draw of the 256 rows and of the 205 and 51, with 73 and 51 on pdz3/single_to_double, which has 124 labeled rows. Three batch orders, which agree on the mean and differ on single splits: on amylase/close_to_far they score 0.01, 0.13, and 0.42. Only the first 100 queries of each split can be compared with the language model. The reading of the control was changed after the two pilot splits and before the others were read.
M14

With one setting run to a fixed length, tuned ProGen2 reaches the level of the best ridge and of Claude Mythos 5.2 on FLIP2, and passes neither

Runs added on 24 and 25 November 2026 (UTC), after the scores of M13 were seen · 16 FLIP2 splits and 2 FGFR2 splits · the first 100 queries, queries 101 to 300, and all 300 · ProGen2-small and ProGen2-base

In plain terms. M13 tuned ProGen2-small under a recipe written down in advance, and it lost. This card asks whether that recipe was the right one, by changing one thing at a time. It was not: letting 51 held-out rows choose the setting and the stopping point cost about 0.07. When one setting is simply run for 20 epochs, the tuned model scores between 0.32 and 0.36, which is level with the best ridge and with Claude Mythos 5.2 on FLIP2. It is never above them. A term added to the loss that holds the model to the protein's sequences moves the ranking by 0.02 to 0.03 either way with its weight, and without it the tuned model ranks the variants of a protein it no longer models. A model five times larger adds little, a lower learning rate and a low-rank update do worse, more rows help the ridge as much as the tuning, and on the newer FGFR2 data the tuned model stays behind both on the queries the language model answered.

Question
Was the tuning of M13 run at the right scale? In turn: does the gap to the ridge come from the shift between a split's examples and its test queries, from how the checkpoint is chosen, from the learning rate, from moving every weight, from the number of rows, from the size of the model, from the spread between runs, or from a loss that leaves the likelihood of the protein free to fall?
Model
ProGen2-small as in M13, and ProGen2-base, 764,803,616 weights, from a pinned copy of the released weights checked against its authors' reference score. Claude Mythos 5.2 and the ridges are those of M1 and M3. For the held-out rows the ridges are fit again, on the 205 rows the tuning fits on, from the features that B1 stored.
Data
The tasks of M13: the same 256 rows, the same division into 205 and 51, and the same queries. One run uses the larger example set of each split, up to 2,048 rows. Two runs score all 300 queries of a split and not only the first 100.
Steps
  1. Fit every baseline on the 205 tuning rows of each split and score it on the 51 held-out rows, beside the tuned model after a fixed number of epochs (the primer, step 8).
  2. Run the ranked loss again under all four settings and score the first 100 queries after every epoch (the trace, step 2).
  3. Run the setting the trace points to for 40 epochs, score all 300 queries after every epoch, and read it after 20 and after 40 epochs with nothing chosen (step 1).
  4. Tune with a learning rate ten times lower, with a low-rank update on frozen weights, and on every labeled row of a split (steps 3 to 5).
  5. Tune ProGen2-base on the 256 rows at the lower learning rate, and score it with no examples and under a ridge on its hidden states (step 6).
  6. Run the same one setting on ProGen2-base for 20 epochs and read it with nothing chosen, and fit a ridge on each ProGen2 model’s hidden states on the 205 tuning rows to score on the 51 held-out rows.
  7. Add a likelihood term to the loss of the one setting on ProGen2-small, at the weights 1, 0.1, and 0.01, and read each run after 20 epochs with nothing chosen (step 9).
  8. Average the reported arm's ranks with those of its other batch orders, of the released model, of the ESMC-600M score, of the best ridge, and of Claude Mythos 5.2 (step 7).
Measured
For each run, its mean Spearman over the 16 FLIP2 splits and its paired difference from the reported arm, from the best ridge, and from Claude Mythos 5.2. For the fixed recipe, the same on queries 101 to 300, which no trace read. For an average, its difference from each of its two parts. On the held-out rows, the mean difference from each baseline with an interval from resampling the splits. For the likelihood term, the paired difference from the same recipe without it on queries 101 to 300, and the mean score of the queries, which says whether tuning raised or lowered the likelihood of the protein's variants. Each read was written down before its run was scored, and all of them after the scores of M13 were seen, so this card is exploration and the reported number stays the one of M13.
Result
The held-out rows choose badly. In the trace, the best cell on the first 100 queries is the last epoch of the lower learning rate with the weight 2, at 0.338, where the reported checkpoint scores 0.26. On the held-out rows that setting is level from the fifth epoch, so those rows cannot tell a short run from a long one. A fixed recipe ties the best ridge. That one setting, run for 20 epochs with nothing chosen, scores 0.32 (0.29 to 0.35) on queries 101 to 300, which had no part in picking it. That is +0.08 (+0.05 to +0.10) above the reported arm and −0.03 (−0.06 to +0.01) from the best ridge on those queries, an interval that includes zero. After 40 epochs it scores 0.31 (0.28 to 0.34), and its difference from the ridge, −0.04 (−0.07 to 0.00), lies just under zero. Between epochs 15 and 40 the mean on those queries stays between 0.292 and 0.329 and averages 0.310, so about 0.31 is the level of the recipe and epoch 20 is the top of it. About half of the 0.07 that the reported arm lost comes from five splits on which the 51 rows chose another setting, and half from an earlier stop on the other 11. ProGen2-base under the same recipe is level with both methods. It scores 0.34 (0.30 to 0.37) on queries 101 to 300, −0.01 (−0.05 to +0.02) from the best ridge there, and 0.36 (0.31 to 0.40) on the first 100, −0.01 (−0.06 to +0.04) from the best ridge and −0.02 (−0.07 to +0.03) from Claude Mythos 5.2. Every interval includes zero and none lies above it. The larger model adds +0.015 (-0.006 to +0.037) to the smaller one under this recipe on queries 101 to 300. With its checkpoint chosen on the held-out rows the same model scores 0.31 (0.26 to 0.35) on the first 100, −0.07 (−0.11 to −0.03) from the language model, and tuning leaves it level with its own score with no examples (0.28 (0.23 to 0.32)). A likelihood term keeps the model a model of the protein, and moves the ranking little. Under the fixed recipe the mean score of the queries, a log-likelihood per residue, falls from −2.12 for the released model to −7.71 after 20 epochs, on every FLIP2 split: the tuned model ranks the variants while it finds every one of them far less probable than before. With the term at the weight 1 of Pang and colleagues, which was named the primary run, the mean score is −1.03 and the Spearman on queries 101 to 300 is 0.29 (0.26 to 0.33), −0.03 (−0.06 to +0.01) from the recipe without the term. That interval includes zero and its mean is below it, and on all 300 queries the difference is −0.03 (−0.05 to 0.00). At the weights 0.1 and 0.01 the Spearman on queries 101 to 300 is 0.35 (0.31 to 0.38) and 0.34 (0.31 to 0.37), +0.02 (0.00 to +0.05) and +0.02 (0.00 to +0.04) from the recipe without the term, and on all 300 queries +0.03 (+0.01 to +0.05) and +0.02 (0.00 to +0.03). At 0.1 the model is level with the best ridge on those queries (0.00 (−0.04 to +0.03)) and scores 0.38 (0.33 to 0.42) on the first 100, 0.00 (−0.04 to +0.04) from Claude Mythos 5.2. Three weights were read and neither lighter one was the primary run, so the gain of about 0.02 is a lead and not a finding. Two changes do worse. A learning rate ten times lower scores 0.20 (0.15 to 0.25), −0.06 (−0.10 to −0.01) from the reported arm, and a low-rank update on frozen weights 0.20 (0.15 to 0.24), −0.06 (−0.11 to −0.01). More rows help, and help the ridge as much. Tuned on every labeled row of a split, up to 2,048, the model scores 0.34 (0.32 to 0.37) on all 300 queries, +0.088 (+0.063 to +0.113) above tuning on 256, and −0.07 (−0.09 to −0.04) from the best ridge fit on the same rows. With no shift the tuned model is behind the ridge on ESMC, and part of that is the model. Fit on the 205 tuning rows and scored on the 51 held-out rows, the ridge on the ESMC-600M embedding reaches 0.64 and ProGen2-small after 5 epochs of the fixed setting 0.52, a difference of −0.12 (−0.18 to −0.05). A ridge on ProGen2-small's own hidden states reaches 0.57 there, -0.065 (-0.112 to -0.021) from the ESMC ridge. On the test queries the order of the two uses reverses: the ridge on ProGen2-small states scores 0.19 and the 20-epoch tuned model 0.34. Averages. The reported arm's ranks averaged with the best ridge's score 0.39 (0.34 to 0.43), +0.02 (−0.01 to +0.05) from the ridge alone, and averaged with Claude Mythos 5.2's 0.37 (0.32 to 0.41), −0.01 (−0.04 to +0.01) from the language model alone: two ties. On FGFR2 the 20-epoch models score 0.34 (0.21 to 0.46) and 0.38 (0.24 to 0.50) on the first 100 queries, the larger one −0.18 (−0.33 to −0.04) from Claude Mythos 5.2. On queries 101 to 300 the smaller one ties the best ridge there (+0.004, -0.100 to +0.116). With the likelihood term at 0.1 the first 100 FGFR2 queries score 0.47 (0.35 to 0.58) and queries 101 to 300 0.33 (0.23 to 0.41), against 0.41 (0.32 to 0.49) there without the term. The lower learning rate, which does worse on FLIP2, scores 0.53 (0.42 to 0.62) on the first 100 FGFR2 queries, level with the ridge and the language model on two splits.
Impact
The answer to whether M13 ran the method at the right scale is no, and the correction is known. What limited the reported arm, in the order the runs show: letting 51 rows drawn like the examples choose the setting and the epoch (about 0.07), the number of rows (about 0.09 at up to eight times the rows, which the ridge gains too), and the size of the model (about 0.02 under the fixed recipe). The learning rate and the full update were not limits. At its best recipe, preference tuning of a generative protein language model on 256 rows is level with ridge regression on frozen ESMC features and with a general language model reading the rows, on FLIP2, and it passes neither. So three unlike ways of using 256 measurements land at the same score here: reading them in a prompt, a ridge on frozen features, and retraining every weight. The plain preference loss also leaves the tuned model unfit to write sequences, since it lowers the likelihood of every variant it ranks, and a likelihood term at a tenth of the usual weight removes that at no cost to the ranking. A practical point follows for anyone tuning on few rows whose targets lie outside them: rows held out from the examples say little about when to stop, and a fixed recipe did better than a chosen one.
Limits
Every run here was added after the scores of M13 were seen, and each was written down before it was scored. The fixed recipe was picked with the measured values of the first 100 queries of these same splits, so its scores on those queries are optimistic, and they are the only queries Claude Mythos 5.2 answered. Queries 101 to 300 had no part in the choice, yet they come from the same test parts, so the recipe still knows something a ridge's fixed settings do not. The 20-epoch and 40-epoch readings disagree about the ridge for ProGen2-small, by 0.012. The fixed recipes ran under one batch order with no control on shuffled values, and ProGen2-base's first tuning used a grid cut after ProGen2-small's choices were seen. The likelihood term was read at three weights on ProGen2-small alone, under one batch order and with no control on shuffled values, and its form for a ranked batch is this experiment's reading of a loss that is defined for pairs. The run on every labeled row chose its checkpoint on held-out rows, the choice shown here to be costly, and no fixed recipe was run on those rows. On the held-out rows a difference is over 16 splits with an interval from resampling splits, not queries. Runs are not bit-reproducible on this GPU: two runs of one recipe agree as a mean and differ on single splits by up to 0.18. No ESMC model was tuned, so this card does not say whether tuning the stronger protein model would pass the ridge on its own features.

B. The baselines alone

The protein language models and the controls for their embeddings, on all 300 queries of each split. No language model appears in this part.

B1

ESMC-600M and ESMC-6B give the strongest baselines, and 256 labels add little to a zero-shot score

16 FLIP2 splits · all queries · ESM-2 650M, ESMC-300M, ESMC-600M, ESMC-6B

In plain terms. Four protein language models were each used three ways: alone with no labels, as an embedding for a ridge, and as one extra feature beside the one-hot features. The two larger ESMC models give the best baselines and are level with each other. For every model, 256 labels add little to what its zero-shot score already achieves.

Mean Spearman over the 16 FLIP2 splits, all queries. The two ridges are fit on 256 rows. One-hot ridge with no protein language model scores 0.15.

Question
Which protein language model makes the strongest baseline, and does it matter how the model is used?
Model
ESM-2 650M and three ESMC models of 300 million, 600 million, and 6 billion parameters, each at a pinned revision.
Data
The 16 FLIP2 splits, the 256 rows of seed 0, and all queries.
Steps
  1. Compute each model's embedding of every row, averaged over residues, and its zero-shot score.
  2. Fit a ridge on the embedding, and a ridge on one-hot features with the score appended, on the 256 rows.
  3. Score the two ridges and the zero-shot score alone on the same queries.
Measured
Mean Spearman over the 16 splits for each model and each use, with paired differences between models.
Result
The table gives each mean. The embedding ridge of ESMC-600M is ahead of ESM-2 650M's (ESM-2 minus ESMC-600M: −0.04 [−0.07 to −0.01]) and of ESMC-300M's (−0.04 [−0.06 to −0.01]), and level with ESMC-6B's (ESMC-600M minus ESMC-6B: +0.01 [−0.01 to +0.04]). Against its own zero-shot score, an embedding ridge gains +0.02 (0.00 to +0.05) for ESMC-600M, +0.01 (−0.02 to +0.04) for ESMC-6B, −0.01 (−0.04 to +0.02) for ESM-2 650M, and +0.05 (+0.02 to +0.08) for ESMC-300M. The ESMC-600M embedding ridge is +0.21 (+0.17 to +0.24) above one-hot ridge.
Impact
The language model was compared with the strongest of these baselines and not with a convenient one. Going from 600 million to 6 billion parameters did not improve the baseline here. Labels add little to a zero-shot score, so one reading is that FLIP2's splits at 256 rows mostly measure what a method knows before it sees data, which is where a general language model can compete.
Limits
Embeddings are averaged over residues, which is the common practice and not the only one, and no model was fine-tuned. FLIP2's own paper fits its ridges on a split's whole training part, so its numbers are higher than these 256-row ones and are not comparable with them.
B2

Untrained, shuffled, and scrambled embeddings fall to one-hot ridge or below

16 FLIP2 splits · all queries · controls for the embedding ridge

In plain terms. A ridge on an embedding could score well merely because the embedding is a long vector computed from the sequence. Each control removes one ingredient: the training, the order of the residues, or the sequence itself. Every control falls to the level of one-hot ridge or below it. So the baseline's score rests on a trained model reading the true sequence.

Question
Does a ridge on a protein language model's embedding score what it does because of what the model learned, or would any vector of the same size computed from the sequence do as well?
Model
The same ridge on eight control features: a random vector, amino acid composition, an untrained network with ESMC-300M's architecture, ESMC-300M and ESMC-600M embeddings of the sequence with its residues shuffled, the same with positions scrambled, and one-hot features.
Data
The 16 FLIP2 splits, the 256 rows of seed 0, and all queries.
Steps
  1. Compute each control feature for every row.
  2. Fit the ridge on the 256 rows with the penalty chosen the same way.
  3. Score on the same queries, and compare each control with the trained embedding it was built from.
Measured
Mean Spearman over the 16 splits for each control, and the paired difference between a trained embedding and its control.
Result
Ridge on a random vector scores 0.00, on amino acid composition 0.14, on the untrained network 0.15, on the embeddings of shuffled sequences 0.03 and 0.03, and on the embeddings with scrambled positions 0.15 and 0.14. One-hot ridge scores 0.15 and the nearest neighbor 0.16. The trained ESMC-300M embedding is +0.17 (+0.14 to +0.20) above its untrained twin and +0.29 (+0.26 to +0.33) above its shuffled version. The trained ESMC-600M embedding is +0.21 (+0.18 to +0.25) above its scrambled version. One-hot ridge and the untrained network differ by 0.00 (−0.03 to +0.03).
Impact
The baseline of M1 is a real test. Its score cannot be had from the architecture alone, from a vector of the right size, or from composition. An untrained network of the same shape is worth the same as a one-hot encoding, so everything a protein language model adds over one-hot features is learned.
Limits
The untrained network is one random initialization, and the shuffles and the random vector are one draw each.

A. Claude models through the public API

A separate experiment: four Claude models asked through the Messages API on all 300 queries of each split. Claude Mythos 5.2 is not in this part, and nothing here is set beside part M.

A1

Through the API, Claude Fable 5.2 ties the best ridge, and the three other Claude models score lower

16 FLIP2 splits · all 300 queries of each · four Claude models through the API

In plain terms. The models that anyone can call through the public API were asked every query, 300 a split. Claude Fable 5.2 matches the best ridge at both effort levels. Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Opus 5, and Claude Haiku 5.5 score lower, and Claude Opus 5.5 refused a quarter or more of its prompts.

Question
How do the Claude models that anyone can call through the public API compare with the same ridge baselines when every query is asked?
Model
Claude Fable 5.2 at low and at high effort, Claude Opus 5.5 at low and at high effort, and Claude Opus 5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 at low effort. Each prompt is one request through the Messages API with no system prompt and no tools. Claude Fable 5.2 at low effort ran three draws of the 256 rows.
Data
All 300 queries of each of the 16 FLIP2 splits (184 for Rhomax), as three prompts of 100.
Steps
  1. Send every prompt, and record the model that served it and whether it was refused.
  2. Give every query of a refused prompt the median of the shown values, as fixed before launch.
  3. Score as in M1, on all queries, and again on the answered queries alone.
Measured
Mean Spearman over the 16 splits for each model, its paired difference from the best ridge, and the share of prompts refused.
Result
On all queries of the 16 FLIP2 splits, Claude Fable 5.2 reaches 0.36 (0.34 to 0.39) at low effort and 0.35 (0.32 to 0.37) at high effort. The best ridge on all queries, on one-hot features with the ESMC-600M score, reaches 0.36 (0.33 to 0.38). The paired differences are +0.01 (−0.01 to +0.04) at low effort and −0.01 (−0.03 to +0.02) at high effort, both ties. Over three draws of the 256 rows the low-effort mean is 0.36 (0.33 to 0.38). Claude Opus 5.5 scores 0.25 at low effort (−0.10 [−0.13 to −0.08] from the best ridge) and 0.22 at high effort, Claude Opus 5 0.26 (−0.09 [−0.12 to −0.06]), and Claude Haiku 5.5 0.18 (−0.18 [−0.21 to −0.15]), where one-hot ridge scores 0.15. Refused prompts, over every arm: Claude Fable 5.2 11 of 513 at low effort and 4 of 106 at high effort, Claude Opus 5.5 68 of 265 and 21 of 53, Claude Opus 5 1 of 106, and Claude Haiku 5.5 0 of 106. On the 3,666 queries that Claude Opus 5.5 answered at low effort it scores 0.31, and the best ridge scores 0.34 on the same ones. On the FGFR2 splits, all queries, Claude Fable 5.2 scores 0.42 at low and 0.46 at high effort, and the best ridge there 0.46, a difference at low effort of −0.03 (−0.10 to +0.03). The average of its ranking and the best ridge's reaches 0.40 (0.38 to 0.43), which is +0.04 (+0.02 to +0.05) above the model and +0.05 (+0.04 to +0.06) above the ridge.
Impact
The model on the public API, asked every query of every split, lands on the best ridge. The ability belongs to the newest model: the three others are below the same ridge with intervals that exclude zero. For anyone running this through the API, refusals are a real cost, and part of Claude Opus 5.5's low score is refused prompts and not wrong rankings.
Limits
The effort chosen on validation rows for the API was high, and low effort scored higher on test rows, so both are given and neither is picked after the fact. A refused prompt lowers a model's score for a reason that is not its skill, which is why panel B exists.
A2

Shuffled values drop Claude Fable 5.2 below its score with no examples, and reversed values reverse it

16 FLIP2 splits · all queries · arm k256_shuffled · Claude Fable 5.2 through the API

In plain terms. Real rows should help. Rows whose values are given to the wrong variants say nothing about which variant is better, and a model that ignored them would score what it scores with no rows. Claude Fable 5.2 scores less than that. It trusts the rows it is shown, even when they mislead.

Question
If the 256 shown values are given to the wrong rows, so the rows carry no information, does the model's score fall to what it gets with no rows at all?
Model
Claude Fable 5.2 through the API at low effort.
Data
The 16 FLIP2 splits, all queries, with the shown values permuted among the shown rows.
Steps
  1. Permute the 256 shown values among the 256 shown variants.
  2. Ask the model, and score its answers against the true values.
  3. Compare with the plain arm and with the arm that shows no rows.
Measured
Mean Spearman under shuffled values, beside the plain arm and the no-examples arm.
Result
With shuffled values Claude Fable 5.2 scores 0.14 (0.11 to 0.17). With the true values it scores 0.36, a difference of +0.22 (+0.19 to +0.26). With no rows and the protein named it scores 0.22 (0.19 to 0.25), and that interval does not overlap the shuffled one. The no-rows prompt names the protein and the shuffled prompt does not, which card A3 finds makes no difference when rows are shown. With the residues enciphered it scores 0.29 (0.26 to 0.31). The plain prompt is +0.08 (+0.05 to +0.10) above that, and the enciphered one is still +0.14 (+0.11 to +0.17) above one-hot ridge and −0.07 (−0.10 to −0.04) from the best ridge. With the shown values reversed it scores −0.25 (−0.28 to −0.23). With no rows it is −0.11 (−0.14 to −0.08) from the best zero-shot score of a protein language model.
Impact
The plain score depends on which value goes with which variant. So the model is learning from the pairing, and not only from the list of sequences or from the range of the values. Misleading rows cost it more than having none, which is how a learner that weighs its evidence heavily behaves.
Limits
Shuffled rows still show the range and spread of the values, which a model can use to set its scale but not its order.
A3

Naming the protein adds nothing once 256 rows are shown

16 FLIP2 splits · all queries · arm k256_described · Claude Fable 5.2 through the API

In plain terms. Two sentences that say which protein and which assay the rows come from were added to the plain prompt. The score did not change. Either the name carries nothing that the rows do not, or the model already knows which protein it is looking at.

Question
Does telling the model which protein and which assay the rows come from add anything to the 256 rows?
Model
Claude Fable 5.2 through the API at low effort.
Data
The plain prompts of the 16 FLIP2 splits with two sentences added that name the protein and the assay.
Steps
  1. Add the two sentences to each plain prompt.
  2. Ask the model and score as before.
  3. Take the paired difference from the plain arm.
Measured
Mean Spearman with the protein named, and its paired difference from the plain arm.
Result
With the protein named Claude Fable 5.2 scores 0.36 (0.33 to 0.38), and without the name 0.36. The paired difference, plain minus named, is +0.01 (−0.01 to +0.02).
Impact
The plain prompt names nothing, and that did not hold the model back, so the main comparison is not unfair to it. Card A6 shows why: the model knows these proteins from their sequences.
Limits
A model that already recognizes the protein from its sequence (M10) has little to gain from the name, so a small difference does not show that the name is unimportant.
A4

On six splits, a zero-shot score with no rows is level with every method given 256

6 FLIP2 splits · all queries · arms k16, k64, k256, klarge · Claude Fable 5.2 through the API

In plain terms. Each method was given 16, 64, 256, and then up to 2,048 labeled rows of the same six splits. The language model is useful at 16 rows and improves a little with more. The ridge on an embedding does not improve at all. The ridge on one-hot features with a zero-shot score starts lower and ends highest. On these six splits a protein language model's zero-shot score, which uses no row, is as high as any method reaches with 256.

MethodNo rows16 rows64 rows256 rowsUp to 2,048 rows
Claude Fable 5.2 through the API, low effort0.160.250.290.290.32
ESMC-600M zero-shot score alone0.40
Ridge on the ESMC-600M embedding0.320.340.310.31
Ridge on one-hot features with the ESMC-600M score0.230.360.370.42
Ridge on one-hot features0.140.080.150.21

Mean Spearman over the six splits, all queries. With no rows, the language model is told only what the protein and the assay are.

Question
How does each method improve as it is given 16, 64, 256, and up to 2,048 labeled rows?
Model
Claude Fable 5.2 through the API at low effort, beside ridge on one-hot features, on an embedding, and on one-hot features with a zero-shot score.
Data
Six splits: amylase/by_mutation, amylase/close_to_far, ired/two_to_many, trpb/two_to_many, hydro/low_to_high, and hydro/to_P06241. The 16 and 64 rows are the first of the same 256.
Steps
  1. Build each task at each size with the same queries.
  2. Ask the model, and fit each ridge at each size.
  3. Average each method's Spearman over the six splits at each size.
Measured
Mean Spearman over the six splits at each number of rows.
Result
The table gives each mean. Claude Fable 5.2 rises from 0.25 at 16 rows to 0.32 at up to 2,048. The ridge on the ESMC-600M embedding stays between 0.31 and 0.34. The ridge on one-hot features with the ESMC-600M score rises from 0.23 to 0.42 and has the highest mean from 64 rows on. The zero-shot score of ESMC-600M alone is 0.40, which no method on this card exceeds until it has more than 256 rows. These six splits are harder for the language model than the 16 as a whole: with 256 rows it scores 0.29 on them and 0.36 on all 16. Paired differences between methods were not computed on the six, so the bands of the figure are the guide to what is decided.
Impact
Within what a prompt can hold, more examples do not change the picture. The language model stays near the embedding ridge and never pulls away from it. The method that uses added labels best is the simplest one, one-hot features with a zero-shot score. On these splits the labels matter less than what a method knows before it sees any.
Limits
Six splits of four datasets, chosen before launch, and the API model only. The largest size differs by split, because some training parts hold fewer than 2,048 rows.
A5

With up to 2,048 examples, Claude Fable 5.2 does not pull ahead of the best ridge

16 FLIP2 splits · all queries · arm klarge · Claude Fable 5.2 through the API

In plain terms. The longest prompt holds up to 2,048 labeled variants, eight times the main comparison. The language model improves a little, and so does the best ridge given the same rows. The ridge keeps the higher mean, and the difference is at the edge of what the rule calls decided.

Question
With up to 2,048 labeled rows in the prompt, does the language model stay level with ridge given the same rows, and how far are both from a ridge fit on a split's whole training part?
Model
Claude Fable 5.2 through the API at low effort, the ridges on the same rows, and a one-hot ridge fit on every training row as the reference.
Data
The 16 FLIP2 splits with 2,048 labeled rows, or the whole training part where it is smaller.
Steps
  1. Write the long prompt and ask the model.
  2. Fit each ridge on the same rows, and the reference ridge on every training row.
  3. Score all of them on the same queries.
Measured
Mean Spearman over the 16 splits with the long prompt, and the paired difference from the best ridge on the same rows.
Result
With the long prompt Claude Fable 5.2 scores 0.39 (0.36 to 0.41), and the best ridge on the same rows, on one-hot features with the ESMC-600M score, 0.41 (0.38 to 0.43). The paired difference is −0.02 (−0.05 to 0.00), and the model's mean is the higher one in 4% of the bootstrap draws. A one-hot ridge fit on every training row scores 0.22 (0.20 to 0.25), and the model is +0.16 (+0.13 to +0.19) above it. A ridge on one-hot features with the ESMC-600M score, fit on every training row, scores 0.40 (0.37 to 0.42), and the model is −0.01 (−0.04 to +0.01) from it.
Impact
Filling the prompt does not turn the tie into a win. With eight times the labels the comparison leans to the ridge, which costs almost nothing to fit. The language model's 2,048 examples do beat a one-hot ridge trained on a split's whole training part, so the knowledge it brings is worth more than thousands of extra labels to a method that knows nothing about proteins.
Limits
The API model only. A prompt of 2,048 full sequences is long, and the comparison says nothing about a model given the whole training part of the largest datasets, which no prompt holds.
A6

Claude Fable 5.2 continues the benchmark proteins' sequences from memory, with 92% of residues right

6 datasets with one parent · sequence continuation · four Claude models through the API

In plain terms. The start of each benchmark protein's sequence was shown, and the model was asked for the next 30 residues. The newest model gets about nine in ten right. On a shuffled sequence, where memory cannot help, every model gets fewer than one in ten. So these proteins are known to the models residue by residue, and leaving a protein's name out of a prompt hides nothing.

Question
Can a model continue a benchmark protein's sequence from memory, which would mean that leaving the protein's name out of a prompt hides nothing?
Model
Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Opus 5, and Claude Haiku 5.5 through the API at low effort.
Data
The parent sequences of the six datasets with one parent, cut at 25%, 50%, and 75%, and the same sequences with their residues shuffled.
Steps
  1. Show the start of the sequence and ask for the next 30 residues.
  2. Count the share of the 30 positions that match.
  3. Repeat on the shuffled sequence, where only guessing common residues can score.
Measured
Mean share of matching residues on real and on shuffled sequences.
Result
Share of the next 30 residues right, on real and on shuffled sequences: Claude Fable 5.2 92% and 7%, Claude Opus 5.5 76% and 8%, Claude Opus 5 70% and 8%, and Claude Haiku 5.5 40% and 7%.
Impact
A plain prompt that does not name the protein is not a blindfold. That is why naming the protein changes nothing (A3), and why only the cipher (M5) removes what the model knows about the protein. The model that recalls sequences best is also the one that ties the ridge.
Limits
It measures memory of sequences, not of measurements. Six parents, three cut points each. The engineered parents differ from their natural relatives at a few positions, so a model that recalls the natural sequence can miss those.
